blocks.text: Geophysical interpretation is closely related to geologic interpretation, i.e., the task of inferring from a description of a region the sequence of events which formed that region. The description of the region can be a diagram representing a cross-section of the region, which comes e.g. from the geophysical interpretation of a seismic cross-section, together with an identification of the rock types. Geologic interpretation is not static. It attempts to reconstruct the sequence of events which occurred, i.e., it converts the signal data from a spatial domain to the temporal domain of geologic processes. Drawbacks of the Spectral Decomposition method:. There is a trade-off between the length of the data window and the spectral resolution. Using a longer window will provide better resolution in the frequency domain. On the other hand, a long window may be contaminated by the response from the underlying and overlying events of the zone of interest. Having a high sampling rate may improve the situation but simply resampling the data will not add any new information. Viewing the frequency slices and interpreting the results as zone thickness can be misleading due to wavelet effects. Frequency Decomposition of Broadband seismic Data: Challenges and Solutions: Frequency decomposition is a widely used method for identifying and discriminating different geological expressions in the seismic data by isolating seismic signals of particular frequency ranges.

blocks.text: Several frequency decomposition techniques are available for the interpreter: each utilises different filtering methods, resulting in a variety in their resolution in time and frequency. One of the drawbacks of the filter -based frequency decomposition techniques, such as Fast Fourier Transform(FFT) or Wavelet Transform(WT), is that the vertical resolution of the original seismic data is not preserved due to vertical smearing (bleeding effect). Application of Multi-scale Mathematical Morphology in Amplitude Compensation of seismic Data The application of multi-scale mathematical morphology which is a branch of mathematical morphology in seismic data processing and the seismic signal resolution improving and amplitude compensation. seismic Interpretation Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning(deep learning, inductive learning, statistical learning): seismic interpretation assigns to extract all the geologic information possible from the data as it relates to structure, stratigraphy, rock properties, and perhaps reservoir fluid changes in space and time. Interpretation of seismic reflection data routinely involves powerful multiple-central-processing-unit computers, advanced visualization techniques, and generation of numerous seismic data types and attributes. Fractional calculus/ derivatives, fractional filtering,fractional fourier transform fractional wavelet transform, etc. are employed for seismic signal and image processing.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_93
blocks.text: In order to evaluate the CO2 storage potential in the Petrel Sub-basin. CGG Jason (Australia) Pty. Ltd. were contracted by Geoscience Australia to predict sand distribution and effective porosities for 400 km of 2D seismic using simultaneous inversion.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report

blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_95
blocks.text: The 2D PSDM angle stacks, logs from 3 wells: Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4, and geological information were algorithmically integrated using Jason’s Simultaneous Inversion algorithm incorporating rigorous quality control procedures to create bandpass and full bandwidth volumes of P-Impedance and Vp/Vs. The simultaneous inversion results are of satisfactory quality. These outputs were combined to derive Sand Index, Sand probability and effective porosity volumes which can assist interpretation. An

blocks.text: Project Scope

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_106
blocks.text: This project has two stages: petrophysical analysis and rock physics modelling for Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4 and 2D Simultaneous Inversion of the angle stacks.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_107
blocks.text: The scope of petrophysical analysis and rock physics modelling is to petrophysically evaluate the provided logs and use the outputs (Volume of Clay, Porosity & Total Water Saturation) in rock physics modelling to check the quality of elastic logs and also to generate elastic logs where unreliable or missing.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_108
blocks.text: The scope of 2D Simultaneous Inversion of the angle stacks is to invert angle stacks of seismic data to the impedance domain integrating well and other information through constrained sparse spike simultaneous inversion. The resulting impedances are to be interpreted in terms of porosity distribution. The area of interest is 400 km of 2D PSDM seismic data. Data are available from three wells (Flat Top-1, Petrel-1 and Petrel-4). The vertical extent of the inversion comprises from ~100ms above the Turonian horizon to Top_Permian horizon. A map of four 2D lines outlining the extent of the study area is shown in Figure 2.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_111
blocks.text: This is the first reservoir characterization project undertaken by CGG Jason (Australia) Pty. Ltd. for Geoscience Australia. The main objective of this project is to predict sand distribution and effective porosities for the sand in the study area.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report

blocks.text: The most important aspects of this workflow were:

blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_113
blocks.text: rock physics modelling of elastic logs to derive a consistent relationship between elastic and reservoir properties.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_114
blocks.text: Construction of a low frequency model combining seismic velocity and well log information updated with rock physics derived property models within the reservoir.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_115
blocks.text: Extensive quality control

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_116
blocks.text: The main added value of this seismic reservoir characterisation project is a greater understanding of the rocks in terms of distribution of sand and porosities in the study area.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_118
blocks.text: The workflow applied in this study is a standard simultaneous inversion workflow. Multiple angle stack seismic data are integrated with well data and seismic velocity data through simultaneous inversion to produce a model of the absolute elastic properties of the reservoir and surrounding rocks. These elastic properties are then interpreted in terms of lithology and fluid distribution and reservoir properties based on a petro-elastic model derived from the well data. blocks.text: Interpretation

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_171
blocks.text: Interpretations were conducted using full-bandwidth inversion results. The inversion results were interpreted in terms of Sand Index and sand probability. The Sand Index highlights the potential distribution of sands by estimating the distance away from a trend line defined in the elastic domain. Sands samples can fall at increasingly further distances away from the trend line, depending upon the elastic property characteristics of the reservoirs. Sands have positive Sand Index. These samples are indicative of the properties of good quality sands. Positive Sand Index values can be used to delineate sands (with associated uncertainty). In addition, the inversion results were transformed to probability for each of the identified facies or fluids. Sand probability was calculated using Sand Index. Probability is more intuitive and more quantitative for interpretation.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_172
blocks.text: The P-Impedance results from inversion were used for porosity prediction. A P-Impedance vs. porosity trend was determined at well log scale and verified at inversion resolution (high cut 60 Hz filtered logs). The porosities were determined from the P-Impedance sections for the sands (as defined by the sand index) using the P-Impedance to porosity transform. Figure 4 shows the effective porosities for sand. The estimated porosities show reasonable match at the well location over the zone of interest.

blocks.text: PSDM processed four angle stacks were taken through rigorous quality control procedures. The zone of interest is shown in Figure 6.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_205
blocks.text: qc procedures were performed for the zone of interest. Figure 7 shows PSDM angle stacks and the frequency spectrums. The alignment between four angle stacks were qc’ed before running simultaneous inversion. In the seismic processing stage event flattening across full-fold gathers were applied, however some possible misalignments were observed. The effect of these possible misalignments of seismic angle stacks on the inversion results was tested at Petrel-1 as shown in Figures 8 and 9. The time shifts were calculated between the pairs of stacks (i.e. Near-Mid, Near-Far and Near-UFar) within the common frequency bandwidths to bring the events into alignment. The time shifts were then applied to align events across stacks where correlations between the stacks were high. Simultaneous inversion was performed around Peterl-1 well to see the possible impact on the results. The results do not show conclusive improvements after the alignment therefore these additional seismic alignments were not applied on the input seismic for the final simultaneous inversion.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_275
blocks.text: The aim of a petrophysical analysis is to accurately compute the volumes of hydrocarbons (fluids) and minerals (lithologies). These data are later used as inputs to the rock physics modeling. The petrophysical phase of the workflow is carried out to provide suitable input to the rock physics stage, as well as meaningful evaluation of the petrophysical properties of the reservoir rocks. This analysis can differ from standard petrophysical evaluation in several ways. One of the biggest differences is the emphasis placed on the evaluation of non-reservoir rocks. Since the well logs are used in their entirety for processes such as wavelet estimation and low frequency modelling, ensuring high quality log data in non-reservoir rocks is just as important as in the reservoir rocks. Another significant difference can be that the rock physics modelling requires mineral volumes such as volume of clay rather than lithology volumes such as volume of shale. These differences may not necessarily change the interpretation of the reservoir but can have a significant effect for the non-reservoir rocks.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_276
blocks.text: In this study, the petrophysical evaluation was carried out where complete suite of logs were available for all 3 wells. Lithology mainly consists of sand and shale. The petrophysical evaluation was carried out using Dual-Mineral models (Quartz+Clay) based on the known lithology from well completion report and mud logs. The petrophysical evaluation consists of estimation of the volumes of minerals and fluids present in the invaded and virgin zones. The volume of clay is estimated using Gamma Ray log. The porosities (effective and total) are determined by an iterating procedure of mud invasion correction based on the density log. The detailed methods are presented as follows.

blocks.text: rock Physics Modelling and Fluid Substitutions

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_328
blocks.text: The objective of the rock physics modelling is to provide a consistent set of elastic logs at each well for wavelet estimation; to provide a link between the petrophysical properties and the elastic properties of the rocks (Vp, Vs, b). This link will allow the elastic properties of the rocks determined through seismic inversion to be interpreted in terms of reservoir properties. This link can only be achieved accurately for full bandwidth inversion results.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_329
blocks.text: The methodology applied was to construct a rock physics model that was consistent with the petrophysical analysis and the elastic properties of the rocks as given by the conditioned well log data. The parameters of the rock physics model usually determined from the wells where the measured data were complete and considered to be of good quality. There was no measured S-Sonic data available is all there wells. The S-Sonic predicted from Greenberg-Castagna (GC) was used as reference in the rock Physic modeling workflow. The model build using Petrel-4 well was then applied to other wells to generate synthetic elastic logs that were used to determine the quality of the data. Where necessary, the synthetic data were used to replace poor quality data and to supply data where they were not measured.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_330
blocks.text: In this project, rock physics is carried out by using the petrophysical logs. There was no recorded S-Sonic for 3 wells in the study, therefore elastic properties of the rocks cannot be understood in detail. Processed and reliable P and S-Sonic data is very important for build a good quality rock physics model. In all three wells, S-Sonic predicted from Greenberg-Castagna (GC) was used as stating point. The rock physics model was built to predict measured Density, P-sonic and S-Sonic (predicted from Greenberg-Castagna). The following paramters used for rock physics modelling as shown in Figure 20.

blocks.text: Appendix 5: Low Frequency modelling

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_367
blocks.text: A low frequency model is required to provide information below the seismic bandwidth. A correct low frequency model will remove side lobes and provide absolute values for the elastic properties that are required for quantitative interpretation. The low frequency model must be consistent with the geology and therefore often requires interpretation and iteration to achieve the desired results. For simultaneous inversion as carried out in this work a low frequency model is required for P-impedance, Vp/Vs and density.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_368
blocks.text: The low frequency model is generated by combining information from seismic velocities, which control the lowest frequencies, and a geological model that represents the interpolation of well data within a stratigraphic framework.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_369
blocks.text: The low frequency model is formed by the merging in the frequency domain of the very low frequency component from the seismic velocities with the geological model which has a broad bandwidth. The merge point is assigned based on the frequency content of the seismic velocity based model.The steps taken to build the models are described in some detail below.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_370
blocks.text: Ultra-low frequencies

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_371
blocks.text: seismic velocity data contain information about the variation in the lowest frequency range throughout the seismic volume. This information can be used to guide the construction of the lowest few Hz of the low frequency models. The workflow for this is outlined in the following steps:

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_372
blocks.text: Extract the seismic velocity data along the well tracks Cross-plot the seismic velocity and the log P-impedance Derive a simple relationship between these properties Use this relationship to convert the seismic velocity to P-impedance Extract this P-impedance along the well tracks Create a calibration factor that converts the seismic P-impedance to the log P-impedance Extrapolate the calibration factor throughout the volume within a structural framework Apply the calibration factor to the seismic P-impedance volume

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_373
blocks.text: This workflow results in a P-impedance volume that is tied to the wells and follows variations in the seismic velocity. In this case the frequency content of this model was limited to 2 Hz. The same workflow was applied to calculate Vp/Vs and Density volume.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_374
blocks.text: Laterally smoothed filtered interval velocities were used to build the ultra low frequency models. Figure 30 shows a seismic velocity section filtered to 2 Hz and lateral filtered at 7.5 km. The seismic velocities show a reasonable match at the well location.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_375
blocks.text: Figure 30: seismic PSDM velocity filter 2Hz and applied lateral filter of 7.5 Km.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_376
blocks.text: Figure 31: P-Velocity to elastic property transform for P-Impedance, Vp/Vs and Density.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_377
blocks.text: Figure 32: Final calibrated P-Impedance Ultra Low Frequency model.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_378
blocks.text: Solid Model building

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_379
blocks.text: A solid earth model was built using refined horizon interpretations. The solid model comprises layers bounded by horizons; and microlayers within the layers. The microlayering scheme can be chosen that best represents geological (structural and/or depositional) patterns as evident in the seismic. Figure 33 illustrates the solid model built. Layers defined by the 9 horizons were assigned microlayering stratigraphy defined as “proportional to top and base”, below Intra_Limestone horizon, the microlayering was “parallel to top”.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_380
blocks.text: Figure 33: The solid model on Line GA336_107.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_381
blocks.text: Well log interpolation

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_382
blocks.text: Property trend models were built by interpolating wireline data (P-impedance, Vp/Vs and Density) across the line extents. Prior to interpolation, the logs were extended beyond TD using pseudo logs from the ultra-low frequency model for P-Impedance, Vp/Vs and Density (Figure 34).

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_383
blocks.text: The solid model was used in the interpolations. The logs were interpolated along the microlayers of the solid model. A natural neighbour algorithm was used for interpolation. The trend models were filtered to high-cut 8Hz for use in Simultaneous Inversion. P-Impedance low frequency trend model is illustrated in Figure 35.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_384
blocks.text: Figure 34: Extended P-impedance and Vp/Vs logs.

blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_387
blocks.text: Low Frequency Model

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_388
blocks.text: The final low frequency model was generated using ultra low frequency models from seismic velocities and property trend models from well log interpolation (P-impedance, Vp/Vs and Density). The 0-2 Hz frequency content was taken from Ultra low frequency model while 2-8Hz was used from the well log interpolation. blocks.text: Simultaneous angle dependent seismic inversion converts the seismic reflectivity of multiple partial angle stacks to elastic property contrasts and simultaneous integrates low frequency information to produce a broadband model of the elastic properties of the subsurface. The output of the inversion is controlled by constraints and settings that are optimised based on comparisons at the well locations and other quality controls. blocks.text: Appendix 8: Interpretation

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_461
blocks.text: Interpretation of the inversion results here is carried out using deterministic and probabilistic approaches. In the deterministic approach a Sand Index is created that identifies sand versus shale. In the probabilistic approach the probability of sand is estimated. Effective porosity volume was also estimated using full bandwidth P-Impedance volume.

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_462
blocks.text: Sand Index

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_463
blocks.text: The Sand Index is an attribute designed to highlight the locations where the inversion results show an increased likelihood of encountering sands and/or hydrocarbons. A full bandwidth Sand Index was therefore calculated as a distance of separation of samples from a trend line established on an elastic property cross-plot. Low P-impedance and Vp/Vs samples have positive Sand Index. These may represent good quality sands. Sand Index based interpretation is shown in Figure 47 through 47. We started with well base feasibility using high cut filter logs at 60 Hz. The trend line use to separate sand and shale. The final sand index volume shows good match at the well location.

blocks.text: Sand Probability

blocks.doc_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report
blocks.block_id: 2D_Simultaneous_Inversion_Bonaparte_Basin_project_report_470
blocks.text: The Sand Index is strongly focused on highlighting areas of potential sand. The downside is that it is a qualitative parameter, which is not particularly intuitive. Probability is more intuitive and more quantitative. In addition, the inversion results can be transformed to probability for each of the identified facies. Sand probability was calculated using sand index volume. The probability density functions (PDFs) were designed for sands and shales. These PDFs were then converted to cumulative density functions (CDFs). The CDFs were then applied to sand index sections to get the sand probability volume. These PDFs were adjusted until the results were consistent with the known well facies. The final PDFs used for generating probability volumes for each of the facies are shown in Figure 50.

doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_0
blocks.text: A decade of marine seismic technology development from an oil company perspective. What does the future hold?

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_1
blocks.text: Per Eivind Dhelie*, Vidar Danielsen & Jan Erik Lie (Lundin Norway)

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_2
blocks.text: Summary

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_3
blocks.text: The history of Lundin Norway dates back to 2004 starting with a handful of employees with an

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_4
blocks.text: overwhelming appetite for seismic data and exploration. From the very beginning until today, seismic data has been and still is the primary tool for finding and discovering new fields. This is probably not unique or very different to most other oil exploration companies, but what makes Lundin and our history a bit different is the way we see and use the data–never believing that we cannot get more out of what we already have, by constantly re-processing, re-acquiring and trying new and different tools, with a desire to find new ways of using and seeing things in the data. There is no best practice in our work,

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_5
blocks.text: only better practice and reprocessing is not a project from a to z, merely part of an always ongoing effort to continuously improve the seismic images. Lundin Norway has also always had appetite for new technologies and have been in the forefront of many new seismic developments. Since the discovery of Edvard Grieg (LUNO) back in 2007, the Utsira High became a seismic laboratory both for 2D and 3D image testing. Directly following the discovery of the Luno field Lundin Norway commenced acquisition of the 1st high density OBC survey on the Utsira High, LN0803, approx. 50sqkm of 200x25m dense 4C OBC data. This dataset paved the way for several good appraisal wells and has been used to push for low frequency signal and provided a fundamental understanding of the image challenges in the area. The dataset is still today, 10 years later, constantly under re-processing and scrutinization for comparison to other new and different tools. A year later, in 2009, Lundin Norway was the first company in the world to acquire 3D dual-sensor deghosted Geostreamer data, LN0902. Over 1650km2 of new (revolutionary) technology data. Like the OBC data, this is still today, a decade later actively used every single day to explore and develop further the Edvard Grieg field and the surrounding areas. A few years later, in 2012, another contractor launched their BroadSeis combined with Broadsource full deghosting technology based on pressure only sensors.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_6
blocks.text: Also this time, Lundin Norway were first adopters and went ahead and acquired over 2500km2 of high density 3D data–as the first company in the world to use this technology. The desire to seek the unknown and the new, is not by luck, but by desire and understanding, and the will to go further and beyond what other companies can and are willing to do. The list of new technology embarking’s is long; MagSeis, Snake Streamer, IsoMetrix, TopSeis (2016/2017/2018), inApril, Compact small point sources (2016) (1/3 of conventional source outputs), Triple source, Hexasource (2018.2019) and now lastly the TopSeis 2 hexasource in addition to very recently also testing the Source Isolation technology.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_7
blocks.text: This paper does not intent to recap all and everything from each and all these different technologies, but will instead shed light on the why’s, the what’s and the how’s of developing and taking part in all these new novel acquisition and processing technologies and how they have actively led to more and better discoveries. Without trying to predict the future, we will also, based on the history, try to discuss what we think the future of seismic exploration may hold, at least on the Norwegian Continental Shelf.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_8
blocks.text: The first steps of Broadband seismic across the Southern Utsira High

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_9
blocks.text: Since the first license commitment from Lundin Norway on the Norwegian Continental Shelf, license PL338 (Luno–Edvard Grieg) in 2005, seismic data massaging and re-processing has been looked upon as a continuous process of development. There is no start and no end; Processing, re-processing and continuously investigating new ways to image and develop the understanding of the seismic data and the subsurface has been a foundation for the field development. The original seismic data used to place the discovery well on the Edvard Grieg field was ST9511. With special denoise, high cut filtering and low frequency signal boost, it was possible to see hints of the graben structures up on the Utsira High area. Following the discovery well, 16/1-8, the first OBC survey was planned and completed in 2008. The focus was to improve the low frequency content and also deghost the data using PZ summation. Only a year later the new dual-sensor streamer technology, GeoStreamer was tested in full 3D as the first commercial survey ever. Approximately 1650km2 of broadband data was collected. Lundin

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_10
blocks.text: Norway has always had an appetite for new promising technologies, and are rarely afraid of going “all in”. With the introduction of BroadSeis and also BroadSource, Lundin Norway followed up again in 2012 with an even larger 3D broadband survey, covering all of the Southern Utsira High area.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_11
blocks.text: Along with or trailing slightly behind are processing based solutions that tries to overcome the need for special equipment. Tendency has it that processing can and will try to mimic expensive acquisition solutions like dual-sensor, multi-sensor and broadband sources, by application of mathematical deghosting processes. This led to Lundin’s own Snake streamer test in 2015, whereby 11 different slant streamer profiles were tested to dig deeper into processing based deghosting solutions and try to determine what profiles are optimum for processing based deghosting applications. This dataset has been processed as trial and error by many processing contractors, both as a development tool for them and for optimization of future acquisition setups. Acquisition, reprocessing and comparison to other 3D solutions has also been performed, such as high density 3D site survey data. Pcable technology with lots of very small short offset (~50m) streamers towed extremely dense has also been acquired, processed and tested. During the work on site survey 3D data, along with the introduction of more sources (more than dual source) it became necessary to investigate the general setup of typical marine seismic sources. This work led to studies of source sizes, areal source distribution, making the source both smaller and more compact to gain better focus of the seismic source wavefield.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_12
blocks.text: The initial trial was performed across the Edvard Grieg field in 2016 and was a direct instigator to the triple source small compact source used for the first ever commercial TopSeis survey, LN17001 in the Barents Sea. Prior to performing this survey, the field test across Utsira High in 2016, confirmed that smaller source was not just acceptable to use, but also increased the spatial resolution in the data. This was also confirmed with reprocessing of relatively old 3D site survey data using only 160 in3 across the Neiden area on the Loppa High.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_13
blocks.text: The latest development of both sources and receiver setups is the TopSeis 2 Utsira Hexasource survey, CGG18003, which utilized 6 small compact sources towed over and across a 10 streamer deep-towed spread. This survey is still in processing, but fully migrated fast track images at reservoir level again reveal that dense sampling of the wavefield, from 6 sources shot with only 2.5 s shot point interval combined with a source-over-streamer geometry is yet another step up in quality compared to any other legacy dataset.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_14
blocks.text: Overcoming the image challenges across the Loppa High in the Barents Sea

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_15
blocks.text: Lundin Norway’s desire to really challenge the imaging problems across the Loppa High in the Barents Sea was driven by the discoveries of Alta and Gohta in 2013 and 2014, respectively. Hydrocarbon accumulations were discovered in high velocity karstefied carbonates of Permian age. The deepest reservoirs are located at ~1700m MSL and follows the upward dipping trend towards North on the Loppa ridge. The shallowest reservoirs have been found at only 700-800m. Water depth in the Barents Sea is roughly 350m and relatively constant. Due to recent Tertiary uplift of more than 1500m followed by significant erosion, the seafloor and the shallow geologic layers today consist of very dense and high velocity strata that was previously buried much deeper. The seafloor is generally very hard and iceberg have scraped along the seafloor for decades which have given rice to a very rugose seafloor topography which acts more or less as millions of diffractor points. This geologic setting can generally be split into three main geophysical challenges:

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_16
blocks.text: 1) Shallow high velocities which bends the rays quickly and warrants the use of near offset data, simply because the further offset data ricochets away and goes critical and as such is not usable for imaging. The solution to this is to alter the acquisition setup and use a method that captures much more of the zero and near offset data

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_17
blocks.text: 2) Rugose and hard seafloor with high reflection coefficients sets up very strong multiples and a lot of multiple diffractions plus strong interbed multiples. In order to be able to handle and remove all these strong multiples (often 10 orders of multiples) it is critical to sample them without aliasing such that they can be properly modeled and removed in processing. This is true for multiples and multiple generators in 3D, i.e. not just along the sailing direction of the seismic vessel, but in all directions. This

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_18
blocks.text: implies an acquisition solution that samples both shots and receivers in full 3D adequately in“both”directions, x and y, or more correctly, in all azimuths. The earth’s impulse response does not know which direction the seismic data was acquired in, and it should not be visible in the data either. It should be uniformly sampled and dense in all directions.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_19
blocks.text: 3) Relatively shallow reservoirs in carbonates of varying porosity and permeability. These carbonates have been exposed to fresh water and erosion that has given rise to caves and other permable zones. As with exposed carbonates today, we see that some areas are completely tight and without any porosity whereas other areas close by have large caves and permeable fracture zones. In order to produce hydrocarbons from such reservoirs it is important to see the areas of best porosity and permeability and place future production wells in these areas. This again warrants geophysical data with as high as possible resolution, both temporal and spatial and in full 3D (both inline and xline). Another aspect of this is signal to noise ratio (S/N). Small fractures and permeable zones must be distinguished and separated from general noise and all the diffracted multiple noise. This warrants a setup that provides high S/N level without compromising resolution. Also, because the targets are relatively shallow the stack mute is often at less than 1000m offset. This again requires very short shot point interval and dense trace spacing in cmp domain to obtain good stack power.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_20
blocks.text: With the above challenges in mind, Lundin Norway set out on a journey to come up with new acquisition setups that would tackle as many of the above issues as possible.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_21
blocks.text: With multiples, fold and high velocities in mind, it did not take long until the need for a towed marine solution with the sources placed directly in the middle and above all the streamers was ironed out. However, a multi-year trial and error including testing and re-design should occupy most of 2014 and 2015, including also a number of modeling exercises. Originally, Lundin Norway approach several contractors with the proposal to tow the sources in the middle of all the receivers, but CGG was the

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_22
blocks.text: only one that finally decided to go ahead and try if this actually could be done. Once the 1st trail was successfully completed (in Gabon) and we knew it was feasible to acquire data like this, a more detailed investigation commenced to optimize all the acquisition parameters. 2 years later, this all culminated with the LN17001 triple-wide tow compact dithered TopSeis survey in the Barents Sea across the Loppa High area. Results of this are now showing clear improvement on all the aspects it was designed to tackle.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_23
blocks.text: What does the future of marine seismic look like for the NCS from a technical perspective?

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_24
blocks.text: For the towed marine seismic market there is no going back to dual source technology any more. The successful application of multisource distributed acquisition such as triple, penta and hexasource have proved itself in terms of viability and quality. When it also increases the efficiency by reducing the time it takes to acquire a dataset, this type of marine source setups will become the norm very soon, if it has not already done so. The challenge still remains with some of them to overcome the need for using two vessels, however with autonomous small extra source vessel, this hurdle may soon be overcome. There are promising tests with much longer source umbilicals too, so there may be other was to avoid mobilizing more than one vessel. For much larger areas, the normal survey could include a quarto wide tow source behind the streamer towing vessel, and one could add a second source vessel with

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_25
blocks.text: hexasources in “TopSeis” mode to cover a part of the survey (a field in development) to get the highest

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_26
blocks.text: possible image quality.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_27
blocks.text: There are still a number of companies that are worried about the blending and deblending of the seismic data inside the target level. i.e. that the next shot is fired before the two-way time for the target zone. In the North Sea and Barents Sea, this means typically less than 2s (below the seafloor). Results from Lundin’s own tests on deblending technology does not support this worry. Indeed when shots are fired denser and more often, the amplitude behavior is more similar so it is possible to recover the signal behind the next source before the previous (n+1 and n-1).

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_28
blocks.text: For Ocean Bottom seismic, the introduction of several source boats with multiple sources happened several year ago and will eventually become the norm. The efficiency gain obvious and the sampling desire is similar to streamer seismic. In fact, the industry is more likely to try and save on the number

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_29
blocks.text: of receivers (or to cover larger areas) and instead use many more source than is typical today. Let us not forget permanently installed seafloor systems, where the source effort is 100% of the time. There is certainly a serious cost saving to obtain using 6 sources (hexasource) covering 3 times the amount of lines in a single pass (reducing the turnaround time by 60%.).

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_30
blocks.text: In order to convert a typical dual-source setup into a hexasource without increasing the inventory requires each single source to be much smaller. Typically reducing the source from ~3500 in3 down to 600-800 in3. Quite a few companies have engaged themselves in field tests and studies on the source size requirements over the last decade. Several studies have been published on detailed comparisons of source sized from very large 3 sub-arrays sources (~3500in3) down to single strings and even all the way down to single guns. The takeaway from these tests are that signal strength and low frequencies are maintained every for very small sources. Currently most single distributed sources will perform well in a NCS setting, down to around 500in3. Going below this source size the signal strength is overcome by noise at around 2-3 seconds TWT. This is of course geology dependent, but as a rule of thumb, it seems to be accepted.

blocks.doc_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development
blocks.block_id: A decade of marine seismic technology development_31
blocks.text: There is no straightforward answer to the question of re-processing or re-acquire data. However, a new survey should be able to tackle the geologic and geophysical challenges the area requires and there is certainly a lot of understanding to be had, in terms of multiples, sampling, velocities etc. that one would learn and gain good understanding of by first going back and re-process whatever data the area has, prior to designing and choosing parameters for a new high spec high density 3D data acquisition, both in an OBS and a towed marine setting.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_0
blocks.text: A seismic Multi-Attribute SandbodyIdentification Method Based on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_1
blocks.text: Teng-fei Ren, Zhi-bing Feng1.2,*, Ying Zhang, Xiang Zhang, Li Jiang1, Yuan-li Ning4,Jing-yi Wang1, Jian Ding1, and Zeng-shuo Qi1

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_2
blocks.text: Abstract: seismic attributes encapsulate substantial reservoir characterization information and can effectively support reservoir prediction. Given the high-dimensional nonlinear between sandbodies and seismic attributes, this study employs the RFECV method for seismic attribute selection, inputting the optimized attributes into a LightGBM model to enhance spatial delineation of sandbody identification. By constructing training datasets based on optimized seismic attributes and well logs, followed by class imbalance correction as input variables for machine learning models, with sandbody probability as the output variable, and employing grid search to optimize model parameters, a high-precision sandbody prediction model was established. Taking the 3D seismic data of Block F3 in the North Sea of Holland as an example, this method successfully depicted the three-dimensional spatial distribution of target formation sandstones. The results indicate that even under strong noise conditions, the multi-attribute sandbody identification method based on LightGBM effectively characterizes the distribution features of sandbodies. Compared to unselected attributes, the prediction results using selected attributes have higher vertical resolution and inter-well conformity, with the prediction accuracy for single wells reaching 80.77%, significantly improving the accuracy of sandbody boundary delineation.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_3
blocks.text: Keywords: Sandbody identification; seismic attributes; LightGBM model; RFECV method

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_4
blocks.text: Introduction

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_5
blocks.text: Sandbodies are an important component of oil, gas, and uranium reservoirs in sedimentary basins (Feng et al., 2017, 2024; Cheng et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025). Understanding their location and shape helps in better exploration and development. Lithology, a core parameter controlling reservoir properties, directly

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_6
blocks.text: influences petrophysical characteristics and fluid distribution, holding significant importance for accurate reservoir description (Cheng et al., 2022; Chaki et al., 2015). Current sandbody identification methods primarily rely on seismic attribute analysis and seismic inversion techniques, which acquire lithological information by establishing statistical relationships between lithology and petrophysical parameters or inversion parameters (Garia et al., 2021). Han (2021) revealed the

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_7
blocks.text: Manuscript received by the Editor March 19, 2025; revised manuscript received August 31, 2025

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_8
blocks.text: lithofacies development pattern and predicted sandbody development zones in the Yingcheng Formation of the Xuxi area based on multi-attribute analysis. Zhang et al. (2024) analyzed the connectivity of shallow sandbodies in the Bohai Depression using seismic fusion attributes. While these methods have yielded robust outcomes in specific geological contexts, their application faces significant limitations. Conventional methods are highly dependent on data quality and inversion accuracy. Furthermore, noise interference and inversion uncertainties during actual seismic data processing often reduce prediction reliability, making it difficult to meet the demands of detailed reservoir characterization (Fan et al., 2023).

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_9
blocks.text: Machine learning methods, owing to their powerful data mining capabilities, demonstrate significant advantages in pattern recognition and classification prediction. By training models on known data, this approach enables reliable prediction in unknown regions (Jiang et al., 2024; Chenin et al., 2020). In hydrocarbon exploration, Othman et al. (2021) predicted reservoir properties using seismic amplitude data via a probabilistic neural network (PNN) algorithm. Xiong et al. (2021) utilized bidirectional long short-term memory neural networks for lithofacies prediction in areas with sparse well control. Extensive research shows that LightGBM, as an efficient gradient boosting decision tree framework, outperforms traditional machine learning algorithms in training speed, accuracy, and memory efficiency. The framework employs a histogram algorithm for feature parallel optimization, significantly enhancing computational efficiency. Addressing the characteristics of large seismic data volumes and high feature dimensionality, LightGBM proposes two innovative algorithms: Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) and Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB). These optimize the computational process from the dimensions of sample sampling and feature handling, respectively, substantially improving computational efficiency while maintaining prediction accuracy.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_10
blocks.text: Compared to raw seismic data, seismic attributes exhibit higher sensitivity to variations in reservoir properties and lithology, effectively revealing implicit geological features within the reservoir, and hold significant application value in reservoir prediction and lithology identification. The nonlinear relationship between seismic attributes and sandbodies is the core issue in sandbody identification research (Sun et al. 2025; Jiang et al. 2024). Notwithstanding, a single

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_11
blocks.text: seismic attribute is insufficient for accurate sandbody prediction, while combining too many attributes may introduce information redundancy, reducing model generalization. Conventional methods typically rely on cross-plot analysis of seismic attributes or elastic parameters for lithology identification, but this approach has clear limitations: firstly, elastic parameters for different lithologies often exhibit overlapping regions; secondly, cross-plot interpretation heavily relies on manual identification, which is subjective and has poor reproducibility (Yan 2022). Consequently, constructing an optimal seismic attribute subset is crucial for improving the sandbody identification accuracy of machine learning models. The RFECV algorithm effectively selects the most representative subset of features by recursively eliminating redundant ones and incorporating cross-validation to evaluate model performance. Its model-agnostic nature, not relying on any specific machine learning algorithm, enhances the stability and generalization capability of feature selection. In the context of sandbody identification, this method can effectively address the challenges posed by high-dimensional data, providing robust and interpretable feature selection results with significant practical value (Wang et al., 2019).

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_12
blocks.text: Consequently, we propose a solution based on the LightGBM machine learning algorithm. This method employs RFECV technology for optimized seismic attribute selection and utilizes a grid search strategy for model parameter tuning, ultimately constructing a high-precision sandbody identification model. Practical application demonstrates that this method can effectively identify sandbody distribution features in seismic sections, with prediction results showing good agreement with measured data, validating the method's practicality and reliability.

blocks.text: Well-to-seismic Matching

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_15
blocks.text: Supervised machine learning algorithms require a sample set with calibrated labels for training (Silveira et al., 2024). Consequently, well log lithology data with known sandbody information is essential for machine learning-based sandbody identification. To integrate sandbody information with seismic attribute data, wellto-seismic matching is necessary. Based on the time-

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_16
blocks.text: depth conversion relationship obtained from well-toseismic calibration, well log lithology data in the depth domain is converted to the time domain. Due to differing sampling rates between well log and seismic data, the well log data must be resampled according to the seismic data's sampling rate to achieve consistency in the time domain (Kumar et al., 2018; He et al., 2020). Using the inline and crossline values of the wells, multiple seismic attributes and elastic parameters are extracted point-by-

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_17
blocks.text: point from the adjacent seismic traces as features for lithology samples. These are combined with the timeconverted and resampled well log lithology data to form the initial seismic attribute sample set. As shown in Fig. 1, the sample set is based on individual sampling points, with corresponding data including time-domain data, lithology data, seismic attributes, and elastic parameters for that point.

blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_18
blocks.text: Fig. 1 Schematic diagram of typical well-log and seismic data matching results. On the far left is lithology, where blue represents mudstone and yellow represents sandstone. From left to right are: natural gamma, instantaneous amplitude, P-wave impedance, and 24 Hz frequency-divided energy.

blocks.text: seismic Attribute Optimization

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_20
blocks.text: seismic attributes refer to special measures derived through mathematical transformations, describing seismic waves in geometric, dynamic, and statistical aspects, capable of characterizing reservoir structure, properties, and lithology. They can be classified into phase attributes, amplitude attributes, absorption attenuation attributes, and frequency attributes.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_21
blocks.text: Attributes like amplitude, frequency, phase, P-wave and S-wave velocity, acoustic impedance, and absorption coefficient are primarily used for lithology and reservoir characterization interpretation. A single seismic attribute is easily influenced by sand-mudstone configurations, limiting sandbody identification accuracy and often leading to ambiguity. Inputting an excessive number of seismic attributes can also degrade machine learning

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_22
blocks.text: performance, as not all attributes positively contribute to sandbody identification (Li et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2023). Consequently, when handling multiple seismic attribute features, it is necessary to optimize and select attributes highly correlated with sandbodies. This reduces the training data size, accelerates model training, avoids insufficient features from a single attribute, and prevents overfitting (Huang et al., 2025). Recursive Feature Elimination with Cross-Validation (RFECV) is a feature selection technique combining Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) and Cross-Validation (CV), designed to automatically determine the optimal number of features. This algorithm does not require pre-setting the number of features to retain; instead, it dynamically determines the optimal feature count through cross­validation. It supports any supervised learning model that provides feature importance scores and exhibits good model generalization. Hence, the RFECV algorithm is used to optimize seismic attributes, selecting those highly correlated with sandbodies. The RFECV process can be summarized in the following steps:

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_23
blocks.text: Initialization: Given the training dataset X ∈ R^n*m (n: number of samples, m: number of original features) and labels y, select a supervised learning model capable of outputting feature importance, set the number of cross-validation folds k, and define the number of features to remove per iteration.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_24
blocks.text: Feature Importance Calculation & Ranking: Train the base model M on the full feature set X, employing cross-validation to avoid initial overfitting. Extract feature importance scores S = {s1, s2,..., sm} based on the model's characteristics. Rank features in descending order of importance score S, generating the ranked list F_rank = [f(1), f(2),..., f(m)], where f(1) is the most important feature.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_25
blocks.text: Recursive Feature Elimination & Cross­Validation Iteration: Starting with the full feature set, the algorithm enters an iterative loop. In each iteration, it performs k-fold cross-validation on the current feature subset: the data is divided into k parts, the model is trained on k-1 folds, and its performance is validated on the remaining fold. The average cross-validation score is computed to assess the generalization ability of the current feature subset. Based on the pre-ranked feature importance list, the least important features (a predefined number) are then removed, resulting in a smaller feature subset. This process continues until the number of remaining features reaches a preset minimum or the cross-validation score drops significantly. Throughout

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_26
blocks.text: the iterations, both the number of features and their corresponding scores are recorded to generate a feature­number vs. performance curve.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_27
blocks.text: Optimal Feature Subset Selection: Analyze the feature-number vs. performance curve and select the feature number m_opt yielding the highest cross­validation score. If multiple feature counts yield similar scores, the principle of parsimony is followed to choose the smallest number. Ultimately, the top m_opt features from the original ranked list F_rank are retained to form the optimal subset F_final. This subset reduces dimensionality while preserving maximum predictive power, with generalization ensured through cross­validation (Xing et al., 2023).

blocks.text: LightGBM Principle

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_29
blocks.text: LightGBM is an efficient machine learning framework based on Gradient Boosting Decision Trees (GBDT), proposed by Microsoft in 2017. It is adaptable to diverse machine learning scenarios, including ranking, classification, and regression tasks, and has been widely applied in fields such as finance, medicine, and geoscience, becoming a primary method for solving classification and regression problems using data-driven models (Ke et al., 2017). The essence of LightGBM is an ensemble algorithm that transforms weak learners into strong learners. It combines numerous low-accuracy tree models, iterating continuously using gradient descent. In each iteration, the loss function is minimized by moving in the negative gradient direction of the loss function, ultimately resulting in a high-performing tree used as the prediction model. LightGBM supports three parallelization methods: feature parallel, data parallel, and voting parallel, effectively enhancing processing speed. Compared to other ensemble learning methods, LightGBM offers faster processing time and higher accuracy when handling data with high feature dimensionality and large sample sizes (Dramsch, 2020). This is primarily due to two innovative algorithms: Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB) and Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS).

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_30
blocks.text: In high-dimensional data processing, exploding feature dimensions can significantly reduce model training efficiency. Traditional gradient boosting tree algorithms search for the optimal split point by traversing all features. seismic sandbody identification data typically contains numerous seismic attributes (e.g., amplitude, frequency, coherence volume), often exhibiting high sparsity and partial mutual exclusivity among features

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_31
blocks.text: (Hampson et al., 2001; Dixit et al., 2020). LightGBM's EFB algorithm addresses computational efficiency through feature dimensionality reduction. The core idea of EFB is to merge mutually exclusive features— defined as features with near-zero correlation—into a single synthetic feature, thereby reducing the feature search space. EFB allows LightGBM to traverse only the bundled features during training instead of the original features, reducing computational complexity from O(#data × #feature) to O (#data × #bundle). In seismic sandbody identification, this method effectively compresses seismic attribute dimensions, accelerates model training, and retains key information about formation reflection characteristics.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_32
blocks.text: Addressing computational bottlenecks in massive sample scenarios, LightGBM proposes the GOSS algorithm. Traditional random sampling discards high-gradient samples (i.e., samples with large model prediction errors), whereas GOSS significantly improves sampling efficiency by retaining these high-information samples. Let a denote the top samples selected based on the absolute values of the gradients, and b represent the remaining samples. By combining these two subsets of samples using the GOSS algorithm, the computational cost can be significantly reduced while maintaining the effectiveness and accuracy of model training. The theoretical time complexity is reduced to O((a + b)% × #data × #feature). In seismic sandbody identification, this method prioritizes learning sensitive features in seismic waveform anomalous zones (e.g., sandbody boundaries), avoiding overfitting to stable background regions, thereby enhancing model generalization capability.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_33
blocks.text: The EFB and GOSS algorithms optimize computational efficiency from the feature space and sample space, respectively, forming a "dual dimensionality reduction" mechanism. EFB reduces feature search times, while GOSS lowers sample computation. Their combination enables LightGBM to achieve 3-5 times speedup compared to algorithms like XGBoost when training large-scale seismic data. Furthermore, the gradient focusing characteristic causes the model to pay more attention to the discrimination boundary between sand and non-sand, improving the identification accuracy of thin interbedded sandbodies. This computational efficiency characteristic is particularly significant for capturing weak reflection signals in seismic data.

blocks.text: Method Workflow

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_35
blocks.text: The seismic multi-attribute sandbody identification method based on the LightGBM-RFECV coupling algorithm mainly includes the following steps: 1. Data Processing:Identify the location and seismic reflection characteristics of the target interval. Extract seismic data and elastic parameters (including various attribute volumes like amplitude, frequency, phase) for the target interval. 2.Well-to-seismic Matching: Combine well log data with seismic data. Extract seismic attributes and lithology data along the time domain at well locations to establish the initial sample set. 3.seismic Attribute Optimization: Based on the RFECV method, use the initial sample set as input data to optimize the extracted seismic attributes, obtaining the subset most highly correlated with sandbodies. Apply the optimized attributes to the seismic data at well locations and combine them with well log lithology data to form the optimized sample set. 4. Class balance correction: Perform class balance on the optimized sample set to equalize the number of sandstone and mudstone samples. Use this balanced set as the input data for the LightGBM model. 5.Grid Parameter Tuning: Construct the LightGBM model. Split the input data into training and test sets in an 8:2 ratio. Utilize GridSearchCV grid search to optimize and tune the LightGBM model parameters, identifying the optimal parameter combination to maximize model performance and enhance generalization.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_36
blocks.text: 6.Predict SandBody Distribution in Sections: Extract seismic attributes for the target interval along seismic sections containing wells. Optimize these attributes using the selected subset. Input the optimized attributes into the trained LightGBM model to predict the sandbody distribution within the target interval of that section. The method flowchart is shown in Fig. 2.

This area exhibits a prominent large-scale S-shaped reflection on seismic data, characteristic of a river-dominated delta primarily composed of sandstone

blocks.text: We performed well-to-seismic matching for the four known wells. Due to inherent differences in data acquisition physics between well logs (point measurements) and seismic survrys (volume illumination),, well log data must be converted from the depth domain to the time domain using the time­depth conversion file before prediction to establish correspondence between seismic and well log data. The known seismic data sampling rate is 4ms. Consequently, the depth-converted well log data was resampled at 4ms to ensure consistency with seismic data in the time domain. Grid data sampling was used to extract seismic data from traces adjacent to the wells. Well log data and seismic data at the same time were combined (Wang et al., 2018). As the block is primarily composed of sandstone and mudstone, only these two lithologies were retained. To ensure the input data format is recognizable by the machine learning model, mudstone was coded as 0 and sandstone as 1, constructing the initial sample set as shown in Table 1. Due to the limited number of wells with known lithology (four) and the 4ms seismic sampling rate, the number of lithology samples is relatively small.

blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_71
blocks.text: A single seismic attribute can lead to ambiguity, while too many attributes can adversely affect sandbody identification. Consequently, a machine learning approach was used for seismic attribute optimization. Given the limited labeled data available, the quality of features becomes far more important than their quantity, necessitating rigorous feature engineering. For this block, 11 seismic attributes were selected for analysis and optimization: natural gamma ray, P-impedance, amplitude, instantaneous amplitude, instantaneous

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_72
blocks.text: frequency, RMS energy, amplitude kurtosis, quality factor Q, and spectral energy at 24Hz, 44Hz, and 64Hz. After well-to-seismic matching, we combined these attributes with well log lithology data to form the initial sample set and then standardized the data to eliminate unit differences. To screen for attributes highly correlated with sandbodies, we performed attribute optimization using the RFECV method. The LightGBM classifier was selected as the base model. The RFECV recursion step size was set to 1, and cross-validation folds were set to 5. Balanced accuracy was chosen as the evaluation metric

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_73
blocks.text: to balance computational efficiency and result stability. We performed recursive feature elimination on the initial sample set. Feature importance was calculated in each iteration, and the lowest-ranked attribute was eliminated until all features were removed. Using 5-fold cross­validation, the model's CV score on the validation set was computed for each fold. The feature subsets' scores were compared, and the subset with the highest score was selected as the optimal combination.

Within this subset, attributes ranked by importance (highest to lowest) are: Natural Gamma Ray, P-Impedance, 24Hz Spectral Energy, Instantaneous Frequency, 64Hz Spectral Energy, 44Hz Spectral Energy, Instantaneous Amplitude, and RMS Energy, as shown in Fig. 4. Using this subset as the standard, the sample set was refined to retain only the optimized seismic attributes.

blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_89
blocks.text: The natural gamma log records the radioactivity intensity of the formation, primarily produced by radioactive elements. Since pure quartz sand contains almost no radioactive elements and mudstone contains a relatively high amount of clay minerals, areas with lower natural gamma values may indicate the presence of sandbodies. P-wave impedance is the product of

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_90
blocks.text: density and P-wave velocity, reflecting the resistance encountered by seismic waves as they pass through a medium. Generally, the P-wave impedance of sandstone is lower than that of the surrounding rock formations. Frequency-divided energy refers to the energy level of seismic signals at specific frequencies. Different types of rocks respond differently to seismic waves of different

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_91
blocks.text: frequencies. Instantaneous amplitude describes how the amplitude of seismic data changes over time. The acoustic impedance difference between sandbodies and surrounding rocks causes variations in the amplitude of reflected waves, aiding in the identification of sandbody locations. This information collectively helps in distinguishing and identifying sandbodies within geological formations effectively.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_92
blocks.text: Class imbalance correction

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_93
blocks.text: To mitigate the impact of class imbalance on the machine learning model, Synthetic Minority Over­sampling Technique (SMOTE) was applied to the existing sample set. This technique synthesizes minority class samples to increase their representation within the sample set, thereby improving model generalization ability (Chawla et al., 2002; Zhou et al., 2020). The result of the class imbalance correction is shown in Fig. 5.
