blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_97
blocks.text: A LightGBM model was constructed to establish the mapping relationship between seismic attributes and sandbodies. To address potential issues like missing values or outliers in the seismic attribute data, the optimized sample set underwent data preprocessing, including removing invalid and outlier values. Notwithstanding, as LightGBM is a tree-based model where numerical scaling does not affect split point positions, standardization was not applied to the optimized sample set. The preprocessed, optimized sample set served as input data. Due to the limited sample size, reserving an entire well log for testing was not feasible. Instead, the entire sample set was split into training and test sets in an 8:2 ratio.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_98
blocks.text: The key to model performance lies in parameter selection. This study used the sklearn API version of LightGBM combined with grid search for parameter tuning and optimization. The learning rate was set to 0.1 after sensitivity analysis, and early stopping was set to 30 rounds to expedite the tuning of other parameters. Parameters like number of boosted trees, maximum number of leaves, subsample ratio for training data, subsample ratio of features for each tree, L1 regularization term on leaf weights and L2 regularization term on leaf weights were optimized sequentially. The learning rate determines the speed at which the model converges. A smaller learning rate, combined with a larger number of number of boosted trees, can achieve better generalization performance. The maximum number of leaves directly influences the expressive power of a single tree; notwithstanding, a larger value significantly increases the risk of overfitting. Subsample ratio for training data and subsample ratio of features for each tree can reduce overfitting and improve training speed. These parameters control the fraction of data and features used for training each tree, respectively, thereby adding randomness to the training process which helps in reducing overfitting. L1 regularization term on leaf weights and L2 regularization term on leaf weights serve as regularization parameters.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_99
blocks.text: Lambda_l1 applies L1 regularization which can lead to sparse solutions where some feature weights are reduced to zero, effectively performing feature selection. Lambda_l2 applies L2 regularization which penalizes the square of the weights, leading to smaller and more diffuse weight values across all features, helping to prevent overfitting by discouraging the model from becoming overly complex. By tuning these parameters appropriately, one can enhance the model's ability to generalize well to new, unseen data while mitigating the risk of overfitting. Finally, we performed a grid search for the optimal learning rate based on this optimized parameter set, determining its final value based on the score, resulting in the optimal parameter set, The optimal parameter set obtained is: learning_rate: 0.03, number of boosted trees = 300, maximum number of leaves = 14, subsample ratio for training data = 0.2, subsample ratio of features for each tree = 0.9, L1 regularization term on leaf weights = 0.3, L2 regularization term on leaf weights = 0.01. The ROC curve after tuning is shown in Fig. 6. The AUC value reached 0.823, significantly better than random guessing, demonstrating good sand-mudstone discrimination capability.

blocks.text: The optimal parameter set was used as the parameters for the LightGBM model. The optimized seismic attribute set served as input data, and lithology data served as labels for training the LightGBM model. LightGBM training utilizes an ensemble learning approach with multiple decision trees for classification.

blocks.text: It first selects the feature and split point providing the highest information gain for sandbodies. Continuous features are discretized into histograms, reducing computation and supporting parallelization. Logarithmic loss (log loss) is used to measure the difference between predicted probabilities and true labels. Each tree fits the negative gradient of the previous tree, progressively optimizing the loss function. After training, sections containing known wells were selected for prediction. Based on the inline and crossline values of a well, the optimized seismic data for the target interval along that section was sliced. These optimized seismic attributes were input into the trained LightGBM model for prediction. To predict sandbodies, seismic attribute data is input sequentially into each decision tree. Based on node splitting rules, the data is directed to leaf nodes. Finally, the prediction score sums from the leaf nodes of all trees are aggregated. A Sigmoid function converts this sum into a probability, indicating the likelihood of a sample point being sandstone. After obtaining the prediction results, the probability threshold was fine­tuned based on the visual outcome to determine the best prediction effect. The prediction accuracy for single wells is highest when the probability threshold is set to 0.65. Additionally, the resulting sandbody distribution aligns well with actual geological understanding.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_107
blocks.text: Consequently, a probability of 0.65 is determined as the optimal threshold for classification. Sample points with a sandstone probability ≥ 65% are classified as sandstone; those < 65% are classified as mudstone.

blocks.text: For the single-well section selected within the 3D volume, the predicted sand-mudstone distribution achieved a maximum accuracy of 80.77% when validated against the actual well log interpretation results from the blind well F03-4. The prediction results for all sample points along the section were integrated to generate the final predicted section.

blocks.text: Due to the complexity of seismic data and potential errors in well log data collection and processing, overemphasizing exact agreement between prediction results and well log lithology labels may not yield the best predictive outcome. As shown in the prediction figures for well F03-2 (Fig. 7), well F03-4 (Fig. 8), and the 3D view of F03-4 (Fig. 9), the images display inline slices at the locations of wells F03-2 and F03-4, along with the seismic profile and predicted sandbody distribution in 3D around well F03-4. The original seismic data in the F3 Block contains significant noise, which impacts the prediction results. The sandbody results predicted by the LightGBM method show high consistency with the two well logs. The distribution of sandbodies between wells corresponds well with the extension of seismic reflectors. Overall, sandstone layers in this block are primarily located at the top of the target interval, mudstone layers at the bottom, with sand­mudstone interbeds in the middle. As shown in Figures 7 and 8, the prediction results for slices containing both wells exhibit this characteristic, demonstrating good stability. Unlike conventional understanding where sand­mudstone distribution is heavily influenced by seismic amplitude, the feature importance ranking (Fig. 4) indicates that distribution in this area is most influenced by natural gamma ray values: high values typically correspond to mudstone, low values to sandstone.

blocks.text: Conclusions

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_223
blocks.text: This paper proposes a seismic multi-attribute sandbody identification method based on the LightGBMRFECV coupling algorithm. After performing wellto-seismic matching on seismic and well log data, the RFECV method is used to optimize and select the seismic attribute subset most highly correlated with sandbodies. This subset is input into the LightGBM model for training. Grid parameter tuning is employed to find the LightGBM model with optimal performance. The trained model was used to predict sandbodies in seismic sections from a field block. Results demonstrate that this method can more accurately delineate sandbody regions.

blocks.doc_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm
blocks.block_id: A Seismic Multi-Attribute on the LightGBM-RFECV Coupling Algorithm_224
blocks.text: LightGBM effectively compresses seismic dimensionality, increasing model training speed while preserving key formation reflection characteristics. The RFECV method optimizes the seismic attribute set using a machine learning model; the selected attributes show high correlation with sandbodies. Using this subset as input data achieves finer prediction results. Using the seismic attribute subset as input data and sandbody information as sample labels effectively captures the nonlinear relationship between sandbodies and seismic attributes, deeply mining the underlying feature information within the data. Predicting sandbodies along sections containing two wells in the Dutch North Sea F3 Block yielded results that accurately reflect the sandbody distribution in these sections, achieving geologically reasonable predictions. This verifies the method's practicality and provides a new approach for seismic sandbody identification.

blocks.text: Abstract：With the gradual deepening of petroleum exploration and development, the scale of reservoir research in oil and gas reservoirs is getting smaller and smaller, and the demand for accuracy is getting higher and higher.During the development of clastic reservoirs in the Tarim Basin,the lithology of reservoir sand bodies changes rapidly and the lateral continuity is poor,so it is difficult to effectively identify the space distribution of sand bodies by relying solely on geological logging data.In this study, combined with the advantages of logging curve for vertical identification of sand bodies and seismic data for horizontal distribution identification of reservoirs, the seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology is proposed to realize the quantitative characterization of thin reservoir sand bodies in developed oil and gas reservoirs: ①Through the analysis of sensitive characteristic curve and the extraction of targeted seismic plane attributes, the feasibility evaluation of inversion in the target area is completed, and the seismic inversion results of thin reservoirs are generated.②Based on the results of seismic inversion simulation, a high-precision 3D lithofacies geological model is constructed by analyzing the applicability of stochastic modeling method.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_4
blocks.text: ③ Combined with geological cognition, the physical property characterization of 3D lithofacies geological model is realized by physical property truncated simulation method, and the spatial distribution pattern of effective sand bodies is depicted.Through the application of this method in the study area A, the problem of certain deviation between reservoir inversion driven by conventional frame model and geological cognition is solved. While the spatial recognition ability of sand bodies is further improved, the quantitative characterization of thin reservoir

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_5
blocks.text: physical properties is realized, which provides effective technical support for the subsequent development of oil and gas reservoirs.

blocks.text: Keywords: thin sand reservoir; seismic inversion, geological modeling, quantitative characterization

blocks.text: Introduction

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_8
blocks.text: Thin sand reservoir has always been the focus and difficulty of clastic reservoir prediction. It has the characteristics of rapid lateral variation of lithofacies and thin sand body ( generally 1

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_9
blocks.text: ~ 5m ). Limited by seismic resolution, conventional seismic inversion methods are difficult to describe the distribution pattern and spatial distribution characteristics of reservoirs, which cannot meet the needs of oilfield production[1]. seismic constrained geological modeling technology is based on geostatistics theory as the core, the well data ( logging data, drilling data, etc. ) as hard data constraints, the seismic information ( conventional seismic interpretation data, seismic inversion data and seismic attributes, etc. ) as soft data constraints, so as to establish a geological model method. This method is a reservoir prediction technique that combines deterministic modeling with stochastic modeling. It gives full play to the number of seismic and reduces the uncertainty of the model. It is an effective method to solve the prediction of thin reservoirs[2].

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_10
blocks.text: In this paper, X oilfield is taken as an example. Its structural situation is located in the western end of Tazhong No.4 structural belt in Tazhong central fault anticline belt of central uplift belt of Tarim Basin.The target layer of this study is the thin sand reservoir in the lower mudstone section of carboniferous.The sedimentary environment is tidal flat facies, mainly developed sand flat and mixed flat.The lithofacies are dominated by siltstone, with an average porosity of 11.5 % and a permeability of 15.65 × 10-3μm2.It belongs to low porosity and low permeability reservoir.A total of 8 wells were drilled in the study area, of which 6 were drilled in the thin sand reservoir of the lower mudstone section, and the thickness of the sand was 1 to 1.5 meters. In this paper, the seismic inversion results are introduced into the simulation of three-dimensional geological modeling as variables, so as to improve the prediction accuracy of thin reservoirs.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_11
blocks.text: logging constrained inversion

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_12
blocks.text: Logging constrained inversion is an organic combination of logging and seismic, which gives full play to the advantages of high vertical resolution of logging and breaks through the limitation of seismic resolution.On the basis of seismic data deconvolution processing, wavelet is extracted for horizon calibration, and then a high-precision wave impedance model is established[3.4].Considering the actual situation of the study area, according to the prediction needs, the natural gamma model is randomly inverted, and finally the inversion model that conforms to the sedimentary law of the area is selected after verification.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_13
blocks.text: The extraction of seismic wavelet is the key to the accuracy of seismic inversion. The Ricker wavelet and the logging wave impedance curve are selected to generate a synthetic record, and the synthetic record is matched with the seismic reflection to ensure that the inversion

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_14
blocks.text: result has the same frequency and phase characteristics as the seismic. On the basis of horizon calibration, according to the sedimentary model and fault space combination relationship in the study area, the wave impedance model is established in combination with the calibration well.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_15
blocks.text: The seismic inversion target needs to be closely related to seismic data and logging data in order to effectively combine the two types of data. The analysis shows that the natural gamma curve of X oilfield has a good correlation with the wave impedance curve, and the natural gamma is also one of the important parameters of reservoir characterization. Therefore, the natural gamma curve is the best target of seismic inversion.In this paper, random inversion is adopted. This method gives more play to the characteristics of high vertical resolution of logging data, and has obvious advantages for sand reservoir inversion.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_16
blocks.text: Random inversion can achieve multiple goals at the same time. The well profiles of 6 key wells such as X8, X4 and X3 are selected, and the logging data of each well are used to verify. Finally, the most consistent implementation is selected as the inversion result (Fig.1).The seismic inversion model reveals that a set of thin sand reservoir is developed in the large set of mudstone in the lower mudstone section.The sand characteristics are clear, and the thinning-out point is clear.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_18
blocks.text: 3D geological modeling

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_19
blocks.text: 3D geological modeling is another effective method for reservoir prediction, which can more intuitively and comprehensively characterize the distribution and variation of reservoir physical parameters in space[5].For thin sand reservoirs, due to the characteristics of rapid change of lithofacies and poor lateral continuity of reservoir sand, facies-controlled modeling can be used to realize the spatial characterization of thin sand reservoirs.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_20
blocks.text: The process of facies-controlled modeling of thin sand reservoir is as follows: Firstly, the single well horizon and breakpoint data are used as the control data, and the three-dimensional structural model is established by using the constraint of seismic structural interpretation results.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_21
blocks.text: Then, the lithofacies model under seismic constraint is established. On this basis, the variation function is obtained by single sand layer and different lithofacies. The seismic inversion attribute of wave impedance is used as the synergistic variable, and the 3D reservoir

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_22
blocks.text: parameter model is established by facies constraint. Finally, according to the physical characteristics of the reservoir, combined with the actual drilling situation on the well, the distribution range of favorable targets is depicted.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_23
blocks.text: Construction model establishment

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_24
blocks.text: The structural model is the basis of the attribute model, and its accuracy directly affects the accuracy of reservoir prediction[5.6].Due to the lack of fracture development in the reservoir area, structural modeling only needs to complete the layer model.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_25
blocks.text: In this paper, the single well layered data is used as the control point, and the top surface of the thin sand layer in the lower mudstone section of the seismic interpretation is used as the trend surface constraint. The model of each small layer is established by the moving average interpolation method, so as to complete the establishment of the 3D structural model(Fig.2).In order to achieve the purpose of accurate description of reservoir distribution and quantitative characterization of reservoir, according to the characteristics of thin sand reservoir, combined with the area of the study area and the average thickness of each layer in the area, in the process of constructing the model grid, the plane grid adopts a grid step of 20m × 20m.Due to the thin thickness of the thin sand reservoir, the vertical grid of the thin sand reservoir is divided by an average thickness of 0.1m, and the vertical grid of the other layers is divided by an average thickness of 0.5m to establish the model grid. Through the method of encrypting the grid in the key layer, the fine characterization of the thin sand layer is ensured to the greatest extent and the number of operations is reduced, which greatly reduces the time cost.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_27
blocks.text: Attribute model

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_28
blocks.text: Compared with the conventional modeling method, the attribute modeling established under the seismic constraint greatly eliminates the uncertainty between wells by using the characteristics of good lateral continuity of seismic, which is of great significance to the accuracy of modeling results[7.8]. This attribute modeling is mainly divided into two steps: ① Based on the conclusion of logging interpretation, the lithofacies model is established under the constraint of seismic inversion. ②Under the constraint of lithofacies model, the porosity and permeability models are established by single layer and lithology.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_29
blocks.text: In stochastic modeling, the sequential Gaussian method based on pixel-based simulation can simulate both continuous data and discrete data, and ensure the accuracy of well point data while reducing cross-well uncertainty.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_30
blocks.text: Data correlation analysis

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_31
blocks.text: A key parameter for establishing a 3D attribute model is the correlation coefficient between logging data and seismic data. The correlation coefficient determines the feasibility of multi-parameter collaborative modeling. The results of previous studies have shown that when the correlation coefficient between the main variable and the dependent variable is greater than 0.4, it can play an effective spatial constraint and indication role in the prediction results[9]. In this paper, the correlation between logging natural gamma parameters and seismic inversion natural gamma parameters of all drilled wells in X oilfield is analyzed by crossplot method. The correlation coefficient between the two is about 0.72, indicating that there is a good correlation between them(Fig.3). The natural gamma data volume of seismic inversion can be used as a synergistic variable to participate in the simulation of 3D natural gamma attribute model.

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_33
blocks.text: Variation function analysis

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_34
blocks.text: Variation function is an important parameter in stochastic simulation, which reflects the characteristics that the degree of spatial variation varies with distance. The variation function in different directions can reflect the variation characteristics of variables in different directions. If the variation diagram in each direction is basically the same, it is isotropic, otherwise it is anisotropic. In most sedimentary environments, the correlation of geological variables is different in different directions, so the actual variables are basically anisotropic. On the plane, the range along the main stream line is greater than that in the vertical mainstream direction; because the lateral scale of the geological body is much larger than the vertical direction, the vertical range is often much smaller than the plane in all directions. On the plane, the anisotropy can be represented by an ellipse, and the long axis direction indicates the mainstream direction, that is, the source direction. The length of the long axis represents the main range, and the length of the short axis represents the secondary range(Fig.4) [10.11].

blocks.text: seismic constraint Establish lithofacies model

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_37
blocks.text: On the basis of data analysis, logging data and seismic inversion data are used as macro constraints under hard control conditions and soft control conditions, and the correlation coefficient between them is used as a synergistic factor. Under the control of structural model, sequential Gaussian synergistic simulation method is used to simulate the lithofacies of thin sand reservoir in lower mudstone section of A oilfield. Analysis and comparison of geological modeling and seismic inversion results: The overall trend is basically the same, but the lithofacies geological modeling depicts the sand body more carefully, clearly depicts the vertical superposition relationship and lateral pinch-out phenomenon of the thin sand body, and the degree of agreement with the reservoir characteristics of the well point is improved(Fig.5). The results of lithofacies modeling have more seismic constraints between wells, which reduces the uncertainty and multiplicity of sand body distribution and improves the prediction accuracy of sand body between wells.

blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_39
blocks.text: Phase-controlled constraint to establish physical property model

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_40
blocks.text: Porosity is one of the most basic rock physical properties. Determining the pore distribution of the reservoir is a necessary step to describe the pore space of the underground formation. Usually, before modeling other rock physical parameters, the distribution characteristics of rock porosity are simulated first, because porosity can be constrained by many data, while

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_41
blocks.text: other rock physical properties, such as fluid saturation and permeability, are often related to porosity. At this time, other rock physical parameter models can be established with porosity model constraints[12]. This porosity modeling applies the idea of phase-controlled parameter modeling. According to the ' two-step modeling ' method, the seismic inversion data is used as the second variable, and the lithofacies model is coordinated. The porosity model is established by using the phase-controlled sequential Gaussian simulation method and layered lithofacies constraints. The permeability simulation is similar to the porosity model. The difference is that the second variable is no longer the seismic inversion data, but the established porosity model. The simulation results can be seen: The general trend of the physical property model is basically consistent with the lithology distribution, and the physical property model also reflects the heterogeneity within the sand body. And the model shows the distribution characteristics of reservoir physical properties in 3D space, which lays a foundation for determining the reservoir dessert area and fine calculation of reserves(Fig.6, Fig.7).

blocks.text: trap characterization

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_45
blocks.text: Through seismic constrained geological modeling technology, the distribution range and distribution characteristics of sand bodies in the lower mudstone section are finely implemented. At the same time, on the basis of facies control, the physical properties of sand bodies are quantitatively described. Finally, lithologic traps are characterized in the thin sand reservoir of the lower mudstone section of X oilfield. The area is 25.3km2, the porosity of the sand is 7.5 ~ 14.1 %, and the permeability is 5mD ~ 50mD.

blocks.text: Summary

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology
blocks.block_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology_47
blocks.text: The combination of seismic inversion technology and 3D geological modeling technology is

blocks.doc_id: Application of seismic inversion constrained geological modeling technology

blocks.text: an effective means to improve reservoir prediction and provides a new research idea for later reservoir description.Based on the results of seismic inversion, a fine 3D geological model is established, which is a further improvement of reservoir prediction technology. The prediction results describe the sand body more accurately than the inversion data, the vertical resolution is higher, and the predicted reservoir distribution is more accurate.

blocks.text: Abstract

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_50
blocks.text: Gas-hydrate resource assessment on the Alaska North Slope using 3-D and 2-D seismic data involved six important steps: (1) determining the top and base of the gas-hydrate stability zone, (2) “tying” well log information to seismic data through synthetic seismograms, (3) differentiating ice from gas hydrate in the permafrost interval, (4) developing an acoustic model for the reservoir and seal, (5) developing a method to estimate gas-hydrate saturation and thickness from seismic attributes, and (6) assessing the potential gas-hydrate prospects from seismic data based on potential migration

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_51
blocks.text: pathways, source, reservoir quality, and other relevant geologi­cal information. This report describes the first five steps in detail using well logs and provides theoretical backgrounds for resource assessments carried out by the U.S. Geological survey.

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_52
blocks.text: Measured and predicted P-wave velocities enabled us to tie synthetic seismograms to the seismic data. The

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_53
blocks.text: calculated gas-hydrate stability zone from subsurface wellbore temperature data enabled us to focus our effort on the most promising depth intervals in the seismic data. A typical reservoir in this area is characterized by the P-wave velocity of 1.88 km/s, porosity of 42 percent, and clay volume content of 5 percent, whereas seal sediments encasing the reservoir are characterized by the P-wave velocity of 2.2 km/s, porosity of 32 percent, and clay volume content of 20 percent. Because the impedance of a reservoir without gas hydrate is less than that of the seal, a complex amplitude variation with respect to gas-hydrate saturation is predicted, namely polarity change, amplitude blanking, and high seismic amplitude (a bright spot). This amplitude variation with gas-hydrate saturation is the physical basis for the method used to quantify the resource potential of gas hydrates in this assessment.

blocks.text: Introduction

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_55
blocks.text: The gas-hydrate resource assessment on the Alaska North Slope (ANS) carried out in 2008 by the United States Geological survey is based on seismic attributes derived from proprietary industry 3-D seismic data and publicly available

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_56
blocks.text: 2-D seismic lines. In order to delineate gas-hydrate prospects

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_57
blocks.text: and to estimate the potential resource for each prospect from the seismic data, a method of linking seismic attributes to the reservoir thickness and saturation is required. This report describes the details of this method applicable to the ANS.

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_58
blocks.text: The presence of gas hydrate in sediment pore spaces increases seismic velocities and the electrical resistivity of the formation, and these physical changes are detectable using various downhole well logs. Detecting and quantifying gas-hydrate-bearing sediments (GHBS) using seismic data, on the other hand, is not simple; detailed analyses, including calibration with well log information, are required to quantify the gas-hydrate response in seismic data. The basic concepts and interpretation, detection, and quantification methods were presented in Lee (2005) and Lee and others (in press), and an application of the concepts and methodology to real

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_59
blocks.text: 3-D seismic data was presented by Inks and others (in press). This report is an extension of Lee (2005) and Lee and others (in press) and fills the gaps of previous investigations. This report describes five important steps in assessing gas-hydrate resources of the ANS: (1) determining the top and base of the gas-hydrate stability zone, (2) “tying” well log information to seismic data through synthetic seismograms, (3) differentiating ice from gas hydrate in the permafrost interval, (4) developing acoustic models for reservoir and seal, and (5) developing a method to estimate gas-hydrate saturation and thickness. Inks and others (in press) addressed the final step of the assess­ment, which is identifying the potential gas-hydrate prospects in terms of migration paths, source, reservoir quality, and other relevant geological information.

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_60
blocks.text: One important factor involved in the interpretation of seismic data for GHBS is determining where to look in the seismic sections for the potential prospects. This can be accomplished by calculating the distribution and thickness of the theoretical methane-hydrate phase boundary in any given setting. The extent of the gas-hydrate stability zone is then calculated using measured temperature data from various wells in and around the study area combined with theoretical gas-hydrate phase diagrams created using a computer program developed at the Colorado School of Mines, Golden, Colo. (Sloan and Koh, 2008).

blocks.text: Fortunately, electrical resistivity and gamma ray logs were run in the shallow part of the sedimentary section. Therefore, the required P-wave velocities could be calculated using various methods to convert measured resistivity and porosity log values to P-wave velocities. The method for predicting the P-wave velocity from resistivity using the modified Biot-Gassmann theory, referred to as the BGTL hereafter, is given by Lee (2005) and Lee and Collett (2008). blocks.text: Gas hydrate exists only within the gas-hydrate stability zone (GHSZ), so determining the depth of a phase boundary is an important step in assessing the gas-hydrate potential of the ANS. The GHSZ is determined from the temperature, pressure, water salinity, and gas composition. The purpose of this section is (1) to explain how to determine the GHSZ using available high-resolution temperature data and (2) to derive a workable relation between the depth of the base of the GHSZ and that of the base of the permafrost, which can be used for wells without temperature data.

blocks.text: above the undisturbed temperature. In this study, we did not incorporate the difference between the measured temperature and undisturbed temperature. If undisturbed temperatures calculated by Lachenbruch and others (1988) were used, the depth of GHSZ differs by about 0–30 m. Consequently the top of the GHSZ becomes about 0–10 m shallower, and the base of GHSZ becomes about 0–30 m deeper. Furthermore, the depth of 0°C used in this study is different from those estimated by Lachenbruch and others (1988). For example, the depth to 0°C at the Husky Oil Atigaru PT 1 well is 400 m in this study, whereas it is 405 m according to Lachenbruch and others (1988). For most wells in our study area, the dimensionless time  is greater than 20, thus it is deemed that the effect of the difference between the measured and undisturbed temperature on the gas-hydrate assessment is insignificant. Therefore, wells with highly unequilibrated temperatures such as British Petroleum 31-10-16 and Put River F-4-01-11-13 have been ignored in determining the gas-hydrate phase boundary.

blocks.text: Most wells in the study area do not have sonic and density logs for the shallow parts of the well where most of the gas hydrate is present, and some have no sonic log at all. Therefore, it is necessary to predict P-wave velocities to tie the well information to the seismic data. Fortunately, most wells have resistivity and gamma ray logs over the entire wellbore. Pratson and others (2003) proposed a method of predicting porosity and P-wave velocities using only the gamma ray

This method is primarily built on predicted porosity using a model by Marion and others (1992). The porosity and clay volume data in the assessment study area do not accurately follow the Marion model; therefore, the proposed method by Pratson and others (2003) was not considered in this report.

blocks.text: The thermal conductivities of ice, gas hydrate, and water depend on the crystal structure and temperature of the formation. The in-situ temperature of sediments in the ANS within the permafrost and gas-hydrate stability zone ranges from approximately –11°C to 12°C. In this temperature range, the thermal conductivities of ice, gas hydrate, and the constituents of the sediments are almost constant. At –10°C, the thermal conductivity of ice is 2.23 W/m°K and is 0.49 W/m°K for gas hydrate (Sloan and Koh, 2008). The conductivity of quartz is 7.7 W/m°K (Hartmann and others, 2005), about 0.25 W/m°K for clay (Cook, written commun., 2005), and 0.56 W/m°K for water at room temperature.

The average measured thermal conductivities of sediments at Blake Ridge, mostly marine shale, are about 1.0 W/m°K (Ruppel and others, 1995), which is also close to that calculated using the geometrical mean of the constituent components. Therefore, the thermal conductiv­ity of constituent components and equation 15 are deemed to be valid in this study.

blocks.text: As discussed by Lee and Collett (2005), gas hydrate usually accumulates in the more porous and cleaner sandstone intervals of the sediments, and this characteristic has also been observed in the gas-hydrate accumulations on the Alaska North Slope. Therefore, to characterize the reservoir, acoustic properties of a clean sandstone interval are required, whereas acoustic properties of a shaly sand are required to characterize the seal.

blocks.text: Figure 13A shows the P-wave velocity, bulk density porosity, and clay volume content for sediments within GHSZ at the Arco Till #1 well, ANS. As shown in figure 13A, the high P-wave velocity interval corresponds to a high-porosity interval with low clay volume content. Except for anomalously high porosity spikes, the log responses are of good quality.

blocks.text: It is important to note that the P-wave velocity of the water-saturated reservoir is lower than that of the seal. As dis­cussed in the next section, this is the property that is respon­sible for the seismic amplitude blanking frequently associated with marine gas-hydrate-bearing sediments (Dillon and others, 1993). Although the porosity and clay volume content of indi­vidual reservoirs differ from the typical reservoir properties described here, the fact that the P-wave velocities of the seals are greater than those of the reservoirs without gas hydrate is generally valid in this area.

blocks.text: Usually gas hydrates accumulate in shallow, unconsoli­dated sediments because of the pressure and temperature con­ditions of the GHSZ. Gas-hydrate-bearing sediments remain unconsolidated as gas hydrate accumulates to very high satura­tions. In this report, the BGTL is used to predict velocities of gas-hydrate-bearing reservoirs.

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska

blocks.text: In order to predict the velocity of gas-hydrate-bearing sediments for a given gas-hydrate concentration, the proper­ties of the base-line sediments (no gas hydrate or gas in the pore space) are required, and the pertinent parameters for the BGTL should be derived from the elastic properties of the base-line sediments. Based on the results shown in figure 13B, the BGTL parameters with m = 1.8 and  = 1 with reservoir parameters derived from figure 13B are used throughout this report for the sake of convenience. However, depending on the characteristics of local sediments, different m and  should be used to more accurately predict velocities. blocks.text: Lee and others (in press) demonstrated that reflection amplitudes mainly depend on the level of gas-hydrate saturation, thickness of the reservoir, and input seismic frequency. Figure 15A shows a relation between true two-way travel time thickness of a reservoir and the gas-hydrate saturation using the reservoir and seal model shown in figure 14 and a 60-Hz (hertz) Ricker wavelet. As the gas-hydrate saturation changes, the peak amplitude, as well as peak-to-trough time, changes for a given reservoir thickness. For a given saturation, the peak amplitude and peak-to-trough time vary with the thickness of a reservoir. Thus, the variations

blocks.text: One of the constraints of interpreting the seismic amplitude using the complex thin-bed analysis shown in Lee and others (in press) is that the interpretation depends on the reservoir and seal models. It is important to examine how spatial and depth variations of reservoir and seal properties affect the estimated saturation and thickness of the GHBS. Appendix 2 shows two additional reservoir and seal models derived at depths greater than those shown in figure 13. (Details of the reservoir and seal models are shown in appendix figures 18 and 19.) blocks.text: Because the area of seismic analysis is delineated by the theoretically determined gas-hydrate stability zone (GHSZ), it is important to determine the GHSZ at an early stage in the project. Temperature data and the GHSZ indicate that gas hydrate can coexist with ice inside the permafrost interval. By

blocks.doc_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska
blocks.block_id: Assessing Gas Hydrate Prospects on the North Slope of Alaska_1097
blocks.text: utilizing the marked difference in the thermal conductivities of ice and gas hydrate, a methodology is developed to distinguish ice from gas hydrate in the commingled zone. At the Husky Oil Atigaru PT #1 well, a possible gas-hydrate interval commingled with ice at a depth of approximately 800 ft was identified using the methodology, although there was no independent evidence supporting the finding. The theory also indicates that the ability to distinguish gas hydrate from ice in sediment increases as the accuracies of porosity, saturation, and clay volume increase.

blocks.text: It is assumed that a peak-trough waveform in a seismic section is a reflection from a gas-hydrate reservoir with zero-phase wavelet, and the seismic polarity is preserved through­out the seismic section. blocks.doc_id: Elastic seismic inversion and reservoir characterization in the Llanos Basin
blocks.block_id: Elastic seismic inversion and reservoir characterization in the Llanos Basin_4
blocks.text: The contribution of seismic inversion to lithology and fluid characterization in oil reservoirs is geology and data dependent. Several studies of reservoir characterization based on elastic seismic inversion in the Llanos Basin in Colombia have proved to be successful for accurate description of the siliciclastic lithology of lower members of the Carbonera Formation. Mass density estimated from the inversion has been an important lithology discriminator because of compaction of shale, which exhibits larger densities than sand. In the analysis of properties calculated from well-log data, the separation in property space of oil sands and brine sands is moderate to small. Oil sands likely are distributed toward the zones of lower VP/VS ratio, Poisson’s ratio, density, and bulk modulus, compared with other lithofluid types. The theoretical effect of fluid substitution in elastic rock parameters and density, although small because of the proximity of heavy-oil density to water density, is nevertheless present in these reservoirs. Successful exploitation of the seismic information associated with the discrimination of oil-bearing and brinebearing sands has been achieved via fine calibration of the elastic inversion and derived reservoir indicators and by combining this information with relative two-way time (TWT) location of the strata to interpreted horizons.

blocks.text: With statistical analysis and direct analysis over crossplots, indicators for oil sands have been formulated that are consistent with information available from wells, although slightly less accurate than lithologic (Vshale ) estimation. After lithology estimation is performed from the seismic-inversion results, further improvement of the lithology description is achieved by combining the seismic-derived lithology with the localized well-log lithology profiles using geostatistical methods.

blocks.text: The analysis of seismic-reflection amplitudes provides a description of the elastic behavior of the propagation medium and particularly allows estimation of the strata elastic parameters in sedimentary basins. The accuracy of the estimation depends on various factors such as source energy, offset range, energy penetration, attenuation, target depth, and others. Some of those factors are influenced by the specific geologic configuration of the area. On the other hand, the possibility of discriminating lithology or fluids or estimating porosity from the elastic description of the medium depends largely on the characteristics of the target formation, which determines the particular property relationships between reservoir and elastic parameters. For all those reasons, the objectives that can be reached via seismic-inversion analysis depend highly on the area and the available data set.

blocks.text: The Llanos Basin, in Colombia, is a wide area at the northeast of the country that hosts prolific oil-producing fields. Oil

blocks.doc_id: Elastic seismic inversion and reservoir characterization in the Llanos Basin
blocks.block_id: Elastic seismic inversion and reservoir characterization in the Llanos Basin_9
blocks.text: reservoirs are located commonly in the deepest members of the Carbonera Formation, typically at the C7 (basal sands) and C5B levels. The stratigraphic setting corresponds to deltaic and fluvial environment, reworked through extensional tectonics. Sand bodies are of good quality in general but are highly heterogeneous and complex in morphology. Oil traps result from a combination of stratigraphic and structural features, with stratigraphic predominance. For the optimal exploitation of oil fields, a 3D description of the lithology is critical, particularly to drive horizontal drilling. Horizontal wells have been a key resource to increase production in Llanos Basin fields.

Those studies show successful results in accurate lithology description for the stratigraphic level of the producing members of the Carbonera Formation. In addition, we have found that seismic data are sensitive to pore fluid (oil-brine), although the seismic effects associated with fluids are small compared with superposed porosity and lithology effects. We have exploited this seismic information with fine calibration against well-log data to develop probability indicators of the presence of oil sands that correlate with well information.

blocks.text: In the Llanos Basin, we have not attempted a unified petrophysical-geophysical inversion approach because rockphysics relationships have important vertical changes across the Carbonera Formation as a result of shale compaction in the lower members. Thus, the rock-physics characterization we use for estimation of reservoir parameters is specific to the target strata, C7 or C5B, depending on the location within the Llanos Basin. First we infer the elastic parameters and mass density within a large time window for a full picture of the Carbonera Formation and the underlying basement, and then we attempt to infer lithology and fluid indicators for a smaller time window comprising the target strata.

blocks.text: Carbonera target levels are relatively shallow, between 800 ms and 1000 ms TWT for the areas studied, and penetration of high frequencies is good when explosive sources are used. The common processing sequence we recommend is basic, including predictive or spiking deconvolution, surface-consistent amplitude recovery, and prestack time migration. Dominant frequency at the target level is within the range of 80 to 120 Hz. By the criterion of a quarter dominant period, we achieve in most cases a property-model resolution of 2 ms, the same as the seismic sampling interval. As a complement to a simple processing sequence, we are encouraged to carry on more

blocks.text: Figure 4 shows a typical CDP offset gather after PSTM and its incidence-angle mapping. In this case, we have partially stacked traces within 10° incidence-angle bins, starting at 5° to 55°. The angle coverage is dependent on the geometry of acquisition. For standard geometries, the smallest and largest of the angle bins commonly are subjected to spatial nonhomogeneous fold of coverage generating acquisition-amplitude footprint effects. This commonly has been the situation for partial stacks with the smallest angle (5–15°) and largest angle (45–55°). After testing, we have found better results excluding the extreme short and extreme large angle-range bins and retaining as input for the inversion the better spatially sampled small (15–25°), medium (25–35°), and large (35–45°) incidence-angle partial stacks.

blocks.text: Oil in the Llanos Basin is of heavy or medium API gravity; its mass density and acoustic properties have small deviations from the corresponding brine properties. Because of this deviation in elastic properties, there is a direct seismicreflectivity effect of the fluids in the pores for the basal Carbonera Formation, although small compared with lithology and porosity effects. However, depending on the area, seismic data quality, and appropriate seismic data to well-log calibration, the fluid information imprinted in seismic reflections can be exploited. In general, oil-bearing basal sands at C7 are more likely to be distributed in the zone of low mass density, low VP/VS ratio, low Poisson’s ratio, and low bulk modulus than the corresponding brine-bearing sands.

blocks.text: In our studies at the Llanos Basin, mass density is an important parameter for lithology description because of its correlation with the shale volume fraction in Carbonera basal sands (C7). This behavior is also shown at the lowest strata of C5. In addition, total porosity can be estimated successfully from elastic parameters and mass density inferred from elastic inversion. The direct effect of oil-brine substitution in sandstone pores, although small because of the density of heavy oil, can be exploited by means of fine calibration and horizon interpretation to develop oil-bearing sand-probability fields and most likely lithotype fields that are coherent in reproducing well-log information. Oil-bearing sands, although with significant support
