blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_5
blocks.text: of 3D seismic imaging. In total, twelve superimposed stacked channel systems of various morphologies ranging from relatively straight to meandering were mapped by co-rendering of seismic attributes. Extracted geobodies were further utilized as main guidance for rock-typing procedure based on ML technique.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_6
blocks.text: Petrophysical rock types were estimated on core samples using Winland plot employing porosity vs. permeability and MICP-derived pore throat radius (PTR) cutoffs. The following three major PTR rock types were identified: 2.4µm, corresponding to permeability ranges: 10 mD, accordingly. This outcome was further utilized in training ML on core data to implement the forecast

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_7
blocks.text: on log data. Among various tested Dataiku classification algorithms Random Forest showed the highest confidence prediction on the confusion matrix and was selected for PTR rock typing. Implemented rock type classification showed general consistency with observed well performance and fluid behavior, enabling geologically consistent history-matching to get forecasts for future reservoir management activities,

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_8
blocks.text: NOVELTY: The main output of this work was delineation of rock typing of the reservoir rocks within the channel systems using ML technique. Our prediction model fits well with production data, demonstrating advantages of applied ML technique in classification and characterization of heterogeneous channelized systems. This Is important in terms of evaluation of the impact on dynamic behavior in the main oil-bearing reservoir parts of the case study.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_9
blocks.text: Introduction

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_10
blocks.text: The study area is one of the oil and gas fields of the North Ustyurt Basin, which is located in the western Kazakhstan. The basin remains poorly explored with quite few hydrocarbon accumulations discovered, mostly distributed In the western part. The exploration campaign started since 1960s led to a few discoveries during late 1960s and in 1970s. Liquid and gaseous hydrocarbon accumulations have been discovered in the basin.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_11
blocks.text: Natural gas fields occur at shallow depth in the northern part of the region within Eocene sandstones. Commercial oil fields are situated mainly in the western parts of the basin within the structural traps of the Jurassic section, at a depth exceeding 2500 m. The main reservoir rocks are Early to Middle Jurassic continental and upper Callovian-Oxfordian shallow marine clastic rocks. Continental Early to Middle Jurassic sedimentary rocks are highly heterogeneous, consists of alluvial and lacustrine deposits. The studied area, representing one of the most prolific oil and gas fields of the region contains hydrocarbons reservoired in the Early-Middle Jurassic part of the sequence. The sequence is characterized by development

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_12
blocks.text: of extensive fluvial system, comprising of multiple stacked sand beds laterally discontinuous and frequently intercalated by coal-bearing intervals. The study aimed to examine this setting based on drilling and seismic data highlighting the importance of an integrated geophysical and geological approach to achieve better reservoir characterization of fluvial systems with respect to prediction of the distribution of reservoir rock types based on machine learning models. Various seismic attributes, including enhanced high-resolution techniques such as Spectral Decomposition and eXchroma have been utilized to provide supporting evidence of the development of fluvial setting. Linking seismic-driven facies predictions with logand corederived estimates of reservoir properties enabled to define relationships and predict the spatial distribution

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_13
blocks.text: of reservoir properties in the 3D model.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_14
blocks.text: Geological setting

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_15
blocks.text: The North Ustyurt Basin geographically covers territory of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, located between the Caspian Sea and the Aral Lake. It constitutes the northern part of the Ustyurt Plateau, covering an area

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_16
blocks.text: of about 250 000 km2. The northwestern boundary of the basin terminates against the South Emba Paleozoic uplift, while boundary between the North Caspian Basin and the North Ustyurt is not well defined. In the south basin borders the Central Manyshlak and Central Ustyurt uplifts. In the east the North Ustyurt extends toward the Aral Lake. The basement is considered to be stratigraphically heterogeneous according to seismic and limited drilling data (Babadzhanov et al., 1986). It comprises Upper Precambrian massifs and deformed Caledonian foldbelts, possibly containing oceanic or transitional crust in the northern part dipping to the depth of 11km. The age of the basement rocks is unknown, possibly Early Proterozoic (Khain, 1977), Late Proterozoic (Milanovsky, 1987), and late Paleozoic Hercynian (Letavin, 1980). The basement rocks are

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_17
blocks.text: overlain by pre-Jurassic structurally deformed intermediate complex.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_18
blocks.text: During Late Devonian-Early Permian time the studied region was evolving as a cratonic fragment, composed of platform-type carbonates and elastics, unconformably overlying older rocks. Later in prelate Visean and Early Permian the North Ustyurt block collided with the Russian craton along the South Emba suture and with Kazakhstan continent on the east. Collision along the southern suture zone took place during Early Permian. Tectonic evolution of the basin was affected by the Central Mangyshlak rift system

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_19
blocks.text: developed during Late Permian. The major impact was due to inversion of the rift system in the latest Triassic

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_20
blocks.text: or earliest Jurassic, which caused thrusting in southern areas of the North Ustyurt. With the beginning of Jurassic, the North Ustyurt entered the platform stage of the evolution with accumulation of 5 km sediments. Only slight tectonic movements affected the basin during that time,

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_21
blocks.text: The sedimentary rocks in the North Ustyurt are predominantly siliciclastic with several hundred meters to 5 km in thickness. The sedimentary succession can be generally subdivided into Permian-Triassic, JurassicCretaceous and Paleogenic sections according to lithological composition and depositional conditions. The Permian-Triassic section is composed of red beds, while Lower-Middle Jurassic is infilled by 500-1000 m thick continental, coal-bearing, clastic sediments. The Upper Jurassic rocks are 100–300 m thick, consist of Upper Jurassic Kimmeridgian-Tithonian carbonates and Callovian-Oxfordian marine shales. The thickness

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_22
blocks.text: of carbonates ranges from 50 to 100 m. Cretaceous rocks are mainly marine clastic with thickness in the range of 1000-2600 m. The Tertiary sequence includes thick Paleocene–Lower Miocene and thin Middle Miocene-Pliocene siliciclastic rocks admixed with carbonates and marls.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_23
blocks.text: Description of generalized lithostratigraphy of the North Ustyurt Basin is given in Daukeyev et al (2001) (Fig. 1).

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_24
blocks.text: Figure 1—Generalized lithostratigraphy of the North Ustyurt (Daukeyev et al., 2002).

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_25
blocks.text: Methodology

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_26
blocks.text: For building 3D reservoir model all existing geological, geophysical, and field data were collected for analyses and interpretation. The database includes 130 wells with log, core and cuttings data and 3D poststack seismic cube (177.1 km2), including vertical seismic profile (VSP) data available for one well. Initially acquired in 2006, 3D seismic data were reprocessed in 2012.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_27
blocks.text: At first stage, a structural framework of the modeled area was created involving lithostratigraphic well correlation, horizon and fault interpretation based on seismic data, The key horizons at first picked on the well log data, were further identified on seismic and traced over the entire study area, seismic well tie analyses required generation of synthetic seismograms (SWT) to match the time of the target horizons within the seismic time section. Synthetic seismograms were generated with the use of VSR sonic, and density logs to match the well tops with corresponding seismic reflectors, along with lithological descriptions from core and cuttings data. A layer-cake velocity modeling approach was applied in the domain conversion

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_28
blocks.text: of interpreted horizons and faults. In the next step the sequence was subdivided into smaller units based

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_29
blocks.text: on sequence stratigraphie approach to facilitate the interpretation and mapping of fluvial systems. These detailed well markers were integrated into the modeled structural grid to subdivide the main zones into subzones.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_30
blocks.text: Interpretation of depositional facies was accomplished with the use of well data with core and cuttings at well locations with review of regional literature, followed by seismic facies analyses. Interpretation

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_31
blocks.text: of electrofacies with sedimentological analyses provided key control for interpretation of depositional environments and vertical and lateral facies variations. Prior to these analyses detailed well correlation was accomplished to clarify structural and stratigraphie framework of the reservoir, based on interpretation of key horizons and fault systems. The key horizons picked on the well log data were further traced on seismic

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_32
blocks.text: over the entire study area. In the next step the sequence was subdivided into smaller units based on sequence stratigraphie approach to facilitate interpretation and mapping of fluvial systems.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_33
blocks.text: Fluvial facies interpreted on well data were mapped away from the well control based on 3D seismic data, engaging co-rendering of seismic attributes (Envelope, RMS, Coherence), eXchroma, using time slices and horizon probes and spectral decomposition with different wavelet and RGB blending of the frequency cubes. Interpreted geobodies were further utilized for rock typing based on classification with supervised training, The model was trained on core-derived estimates from routine (RCA) and special (SCAL) laboratory measurements to forecast on log data, Petrophysical evaluation involved results of RCA available in 30 wells and SCAL available in 7 wells with measurements of capillary pressure, mercury injection capillary pressure (MICP), and centrifuge-derived relative permeability and residual water saturation. Interpretation

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_34
blocks.text: of porosity was accomplished with the use of neutron, density and acoustic logs, validated against RCA and CMR (5 wells) data. Volume of shale (Vsh) was estimated from gamma ray (GR) logs with application

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_35
blocks.text: of Old-Larionov empirical model. For water saturation (Sw) evaluation Archie’s equation and the double water equation were utilized.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_36
blocks.text: The outcomes were further applied to generate a 3D static model to predict lithofacies and petrophysical properties away from well control. Th channel part and flood plain background were modeled separately to prevent mixing of input statistics (fractions, variograms, anisotropy and trends). For this purpose, channel part of the model was generated with the use of seismically interpreted channel polygons and corresponding well markers. Initially, lithofacies were propagated into the 3D cellular grid to be used as the main constrain for modeling of reservoir rock types, which were further integrated into petrophysical properties modeling. The modeling of discrete and continuous properties was accomplished by the application of stochastic algorithms to account uncertainty.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_37
blocks.text: RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_38
blocks.text: Depositional framework. The results of earlier studies by Bashimova et al. (2024) presenting the outcome

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_39
blocks.text: of channel belt mapping through the application of Spectral Decomposition, eXchroma and a set of amplitude-related seismic attributes (Envelope, Sweetness, RMS) for the interpretation of channel system were used as the main input for further elucidation of the reservoir architecture and properties of the Middle Jurassic channel complex. In this case study, we attempt to characterize the channel complex infill in

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_40
blocks.text: terms of distribution of rock types and associated lateral distribution patterns, using supervised machine learning classification techniques. For this purpose, a 3D reservoir model was built to reflect fluvial reservoir architecture with respect to the distribution of corresponding lithofacies and rock types, constituting the channel infill and background floodplain facies.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_41
blocks.text: The channel system detected in the study area is distributed within the Early-Middle Jurassic succession, represented by braided river and meandering multi-stacked channel complexes. The stratigraphie interpretation of the fluvial complexes included the delineation of the key bed boundaries and detailed lithostratigraphic subdivision of the studied Jurassic succession, involving the analyses of depositional environments and the sequence stratigraphie framework. The well-tied seismic key horizons were subdivided into sequence stratigraphie units, based on all existing well logs, seismic and core and cuttings data, combined to interpret sequence boundaries and stratigraphie subunits, that greatly facilitated detection

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_42
blocks.text: of channel fades. Sequence stratigraphie analyses required an understanding of the regional geologic setting to develop an overall sedimentological concept.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_43
blocks.text: A review of regional depositional studies in the North Ustyurt Basin confirms development of fluvialdeltaic settings in the area starting from the Early Jurassic time and continuing during Middle Jurassic, eventually transitioning to shallow marine in the Upper Jurassic. Prior to the Jurassic continental arid conditions prevailed during Permian-Triassic. This depositional trend is clearly evident in the lithological composition and sedimentological features observed in the studied succession of the field. Arid and continental conditions in Permian-Triassic are inferred according to red beds development at the base

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_44
blocks.text: of the penetrated 2700-m sequence. Fluvial-deltaic are discerned from abundant plant remnants, coal, cross bedding, scouring and course-grained sediments in Early-Middle Jurassic, while shallow marine can be deduced from widespread occurrence of marine carbonates in Upper Jurassic. Fig. 2 summarizes the lithological composition and interpreted conditions of depositional environment, inferred based on sedimentological analyses of core and cuttings collected at the field.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_45
blocks.text: Figure 2—Summary of lithostratigraphic framework of the study area

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_46
blocks.text: Correlation of stratigraphie markers. The structural framework was constructed based on well markers and seismic horizons, Totally five seismic horizons were identified and picked within the 600m thick Jurassic succession in the study area:

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_47
blocks.text: Top of Jurassic–base of shaly, low density and low resistivity Cretaceous rocks Carbonate Top–the top of regional carbonate bed

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_48
blocks.text: Marl–transition from carbonate beds to clean regional shale Key Coal–continuous coal bed, traceable through the entire field

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_49
blocks.text: Base of Jurassic–base of Lower Jurassic fluvial sandstone bed, unconformably lying on top of Triassic

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_50
blocks.text: The most challenging part of correlation was related to tracing of the unconformity at the base of Jurassic, especially in the eastern part of the field, where the Early Jurassic sand bed pinches out. Important information was extracted from core and cuttings data, allowing to trace the boundary between loose Permian-Triassic red beds and the Early Jurassic sand bed. Overall, core and cutting descriptions appear in a good agreement with log signature and seismic interpretation. The Permian-Triassic loose sediments show a drastic increase in caliper, decrease In resistivity and density. The loose nature of the PermianTriassic rocks developed due to subaerial exposure of the rocks during active uplifting stage. The evidence

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_51
blocks.text: of unconformity development at the base Jurassic, traced on the seismic and interpreted with consideration

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_52
blocks.text: of regional background, core and log data is supported by the analysis of CBIL data. Fig. 4 illustrates position of the unconformity, where the dip angles drastically increase entering Permian-Triassic uplift. The Permian-Triassic sequence is intensively folded and faulted due to active tectonics, associated with compression exerted from the south caused by inversion of the Central Mangyshlak rift system.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_53
blocks.text: Besides the seismically traceable key markers additional well markers, picked based on the sequence stratigraphie concept, related to occurrence of coal-rich layers and maximum flooding surfaces (MFS), were correlated and Incorporated into the structural model. Fig. 3 illustrates the position of the well markers in 10 representative wells of the field.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_54
blocks.text: Figure 3—Summary of lithostratigraphic framework of the study area

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_55
blocks.text: According to the applied concept, the sequence can be subdivided into smaller lithostratigraphic unitis, especially well traceable in the upper part of Middle Jurassic, which is enriched in coal. This part of the sequence consists of a series of repetitive sub-cycles, each starting at the base with sandstone and ending up on top with coal-shale interval, corresponding to flooding event on coastal marshes. An abrupt change from coal/shale to sand marks the parasequence boundary, representing flooding event, implies a move from a relatively higher energy environment with sand deposition to a quieter low energy coal-shale dominant setting, Interpreted parasequences within the upper coal-rich part of Middle Jurassic of the study area are displayed in Fig. 3.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_56
blocks.text: Structural framework. Totally 7 seismically traced and well-tied key horizons and 37 faults were used as input for structural framework generation. The overall structural concept of the area is depicted in the Fig. 4, reflecting the position of Permian-Triassic basement uplift, the development of angular unconformity at the base of Jurassic and generally conformable and gentle distribution of Jurassic horizons. Structurally the area is distinctive in the deeper part of the penetrated sequence, due to development of Permian-Triassic basement uplift. The uplift exerts structural control on the deposition of the overlying Early Jurassic sediments. The Early Jurassic section, largely represented by a braided alluvial sand bed, exhibits pinching out to the southeast toward the Permian-Triassic uplift apex. The 100 m thick sand bed, unconformably overlying PermianTriassic, gradually decreases in thickness to the southeast, eventually disappearing reaching the apex of the uplift.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_57
blocks.text: Figure 4—Schematic illustration of Early Jurassic bed distribution in respect to basement uplift.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_58
blocks.text: The fault pattern in the study area is interpreted as strike-slip, aligned parallel to the Central Mangyshlak paleorift system. The master fault runs closer to the southern edge of the field, oriented in the sub-latitudinal direction from the NW to SE. Numerous splay faults associated with the master fault were detected on both flanks of the fault directed to the NE and SW. The displacement of the splay faults is insignificant, not exceeding 15-20 m.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_59
blocks.text: Log signature and core data. Channel system interpretation in the study area was undertaken previously in work by Bashimova et al. (2024). Multiple stacked channel systems were detected within the Early Jurassic and lower part of the Middle Jurassic succession based on analyses of seismic attributes and well log data. Totally 12 individual channel complexes were detected quite extensively all over the entire study area. The

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_60
blocks.text: channelized complexes were initially detected on the well logs, systematically clustering into individual elongated geobodies akin to channelized systems.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_61
blocks.text: Remarkably, wells located away from the channel system exhibited abrupt sand beds disappearance consistent with transition to floodplain facies. Wells drilled outside of the channel sands exhibit saw-toothlike log signature, due to thin bed sand-shale alternation, indicating development of flood-plain facies. The sand bell-shaped log signature indicating fining upward together with sedimentological features like cross bedding, scour surfaces, abundant coalified plant remnants, including coal were considered as the signs of fluvial influence. Representative well logs, showing typical fining upward signature are shown in Fig. 5.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_62
blocks.text: Figure 5—Representative weil section showing log signature of sand bed, interpreted as channelized complex.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_63
blocks.text: The fining upward log signature is associated with general sand bed thinning upward tendency. The Early to Middle Jurassic sequence shows higher enrichment of sand beds in the lower part, gradually thinning upward and replaced by coal-rich shaly intervals. This overall trend is attributable to the general increase of flooding associated with progressive transgression leading to regional establishment of marine conditions during Upper Jurassic. Development of transgressive trend during Middle-Upper Jurassic is consistent with gradual topographical flattening as consequence of tectonic setting prevailing during that time. Gradual decrease of energy due to gentle topography is reflected in the increase of deposition of finer sediments. Enrichment in coal in the upper part of Middle Jurassic can be also linked to inundation as a result of structural gradient decrease and eustatic sea level rise, accompanying transgression. The signs of flattened topography are reflected in the shape of channel belts, detected in the sequence. While Early Jurassic sand bed formed as a braided river, the Middle Jurassic channel systems tend to change upward from straight to meandering. Continuous sea level rise marked the change from continental fluvial to shallow marine transgression leading to formation of carbonate sequences during Upper Jurassic.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_64
blocks.text: Comparison of core and log derived porosity and clay content values of the sediments appeared to be in agreement with interpretation of channel systems. The channel facies show a higher proportion of the petrophysically good reservoir rocks with higher effective porosity (PHIE) and lower Vsh. Sandstones present in the flood plain facies are thin bedded, characterized by lower quality of reservoir properties. Wells drilled outside of the channel sands exhibit saw-tooth-like log signature, due to thin bed sand-shale alternation, indicating development of flood-plain facies, The overall volume of reservoir rocks in the flood plain is overwhelmingly smaller, To obtain quantitative evaluation of the reservoir rocks distributions within the channel and flood plain facies detailed petrophysical rock typing was required.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_65
blocks.text: seismic signature. The channelized bodies detected by Bashimova et al. (2024) were interpreted as a result of scanning of the horizon slices of the 3D seismic cube flattened to corresponding seismic reflectors. Different seismic attributes were examined, among which the most prominent results were obtained by application of Spectral Decomposition and amplitude-related attributes, such as eXchroma, followed by Envelope, RMS and Sweetness. Interpreted geobodies showed remarkable correlation with log data. Fig. 6 shows example of seismically detected fluvial geobody, compared to the spatial distribution of sand bed at well locations based on well logging data.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_66
blocks.text: Figure 6—Example of a fluvial system interpreted based on seismic attributes analysis (spectral decomposition). The image on the top right corner shows interpreted channel polygon along with fluvial sand beds within the corresponding subzone (red circles) interpreted on log data.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_67
blocks.text: Figure 7—Modeled structural framework of the field with integrated channel system.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_68
blocks.text: The channel belts identified in the Middle Jurassic change upward in shape from straight, branched to meandering. The width of the channel belts varies from 200 to 1500 m, while thickness typically falls in the range of 25-30 m. The largest channel belts occur in the middle part of Middle Jurassic. In the lowermost part

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_69
blocks.text: of the Middle Jurassic, thickness of channels drops below 25 m, that hindered seismic tracing of the channel belts away from well data. The insignificant thickness of the channel systems was the main obstacle in elucidating channel infill internally. Deteriorated quality of seismic in the zone of interest was another factor limiting the application of seismic in this study. The geobodies representing interpreted channel systems, incorporated into the 3D grid are shown in Fig. 6

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_70
blocks.text: Lithofacies classification by petrophysical interpretation

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_71
blocks.text: Four different lithotypes were identified within Jurassic pay zones, inferred from the results of petrophysical evaluation, including sand, shale, coal and dense rock. The reservoir rocks are characterized by average porosity of 14.7% and average permeability of 5.6 mD. Large volume of core-derived laboratory measurements coupled with Combinable magnetic resonance (CMR) and X-ray Diffraction (XRD) estimates provided a solid background for application of petrophysical empirical methods. Comparison of core GR measurements to the readings from the well logs ensured accuracy of depth matching. The highest confidence in interpretation was attained for the evaluation of PHIE. The best correlation with core-derived values was attained for acoustic-derived porosity estimates obtained by application of the Raymer-HuntGardner equation, Vsh values were calibrated to RCA and SCAL measurements.

A wide spread in the combined cross plot for all pay zones appeared as main limitation for reservoir rock classification based on porosity and permeability.

blocks.text: Conclusion

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_90
blocks.text: In this study an integrated approach was demonstrated to obtain quantitative evaluation of the reservoir rock types within the Jurassic fluvial reservoir of the the North Ustyurt Basin by integrating different dataseis including core, well logs and seismic attributes. The outcome of this study enhances the results of

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Integrating Seismic Attributes_91
blocks.text: previous seismic facies analyses by integrating into 3D reservoir model to capture details of the reservoir heterogeneity in terms of reservoir quality to locate sweet spots. The reservoir rocks were subdivided into three rock types: good, moderate and poor reservoir rock, with consideration of porosity permeability and pore size cutoffs, defined with the use of laboratory analyses of core samples. The discrete logs depicting reservoir rock types were generated by application of ML supervised training, implementing revealed petrophysical relationships between PHIE, Vsh, density, Swirr, and permeability. Propagated corresponding 3D properties showed good consistency when compared to the observed well performance.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_1
blocks.text: Emre Artun, SPE, West Virginia University; Shahab D. Mohaghegh, SPE, West Virginia University; Jaime Toro, West Virginia University; Tom Wilson, West Virginia University; Alejandro Sanchez, Anadarko Petroleum Corporation

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_2
blocks.text: Abstract

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_3
blocks.text: Today, the major challenge in reservoir characterization is integrating data coming from different sources in varying scales, in order to obtain an accurate and high-resolution reservoir model. The role of seismic data in this integration is often limited to providing a structural model for the reservoir. Its relatively low resolution usually limits its further use. However, its areal coverage and availability suggest that it has the potential of providing valuable data for more detailed reservoir characterization studies through the process of seismic inversion. In this paper, a novel intelligent seismic inversion methodology is presented to achieve a desirable correlation between relatively low-frequency seismic signals, and the much higher frequency wireline-log data. Vertical seismic profile (VSP) is used as an intermediate step between the well logs and the surface seismic. A synthetic seismic model is developed by using real data and seismic interpretation. In the example presented here, the model represents the Atoka and Morrow formations, and the overlying Pennsylvanian sequence of the Buffalo Valley Field in New Mexico. Generalized regression neural network (GRNN) is used to build two independent correlation models between; 1) Surface seismic and VSP, 2) VSP and well logs. After generating virtual VSP’s from the surface seismic, well logs are predicted by using the correlation between VSP and well logs.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_4
blocks.text: The values of the density log, which is a surrogate for reservoir porosity, are predicted for each seismic trace through the seismic line with a classification approach having a correlation coefficient of 0.81. The same methodology is then applied to real data taken from the Buffalo Valley Field, to predict interwell gamma ray and neutron porosity logs through the seismic line of interest. The same procedure can be applied to a complete 3D seismic block to obtain 3D distributions of reservoir properties with less uncertainty than the geostatistical estimation methods. The intelligent seismic inversion method should help to increase the success of

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_5
blocks.text: drilling new wells during field development.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_6
blocks.text: Introduction

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_7
blocks.text: Reservoir characterization requires building a spatial model of the reservoir by using appropriate data gathered from previous studies. This spatial model is then used in flow simulators, which can predict reservoir performance. An accurate and reliable reservoir characterization study is indispensable in reservoir management. The major challenge in today’s reservoir characterization is to integrate all different kinds of data to obtain an accurate and high-resolution reservoir model. The concept of data analysis forms the basis of reservoir characterization. Uncertainty, unreliability, and large variety of scales due to the different origins of the data must be taken into consideration. Together with the immense size of the data sets that must be dealt with, these issues bring complex problems, which are hard to address with conventional tools. That’s why unconventional computation tools have gained much interest in data analysis in recent years. Among those modern tools; intelligent systems, which mimic the mechanism of the human mind, are a way of dealing with imprecision and partial truth1. It should not surprise us that using intelligent systems in reservoir characterization studies has become a widely-used method in the petroleum engineering literature. Some previous intelligent reservoir characterization applications include, but are not limited to, synthetic log generation2.3,4, permeability estimation from

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_8
blocks.text: logs5.6, and predicting bulk volume of oil7.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_9
blocks.text: Let us consider different types of data used in reservoir characterization: core samples provide very high resolution information about the reservoir (fraction of inches), while seismic data have a resolution in tens of feet, and well logs have in one of inches. Because of its low resolution, seismic data is routinely used only to attain a structural view of the reservoir. On the other hand, unlike core samples or well logs, which are only available at isolated localities of a reservoir, seismic data frequently provides 3D coverage over a large area. Because of this areal coverage, researchers have always aimed to use seismic data in reservoir description. Inverse modeling of reservoir properties from the seismic data is known as seismic inversion in the literature. The process presented in this paper includes modeling of the well logs from seismic data, which is also an inverse modeling process (Figure 1). This approach attracts a lot of interest and is very important because of the necessary shift from exploration to development of existing fields8.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_10
blocks.text: seismic inversion has been applied by several authors with different approaches. Hampson et al.8 and Leiphart and Hart9

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_11
blocks.text: have compared different techniques such as multiple linear regression, backpropagation and probabilistic neural networks. They have predicted porosity logs from seismic attributes and both have suggested using probabilistic neural networks in this type of problems considering its mathematical simplicity and success.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_12
blocks.text: Balch et al.10 have used fuzzy ranking to see which type of seismic attribute is related to the target reservoir property. They have modeled correlations between those selected attributes and porosity, water saturation and net pay thickness by using a backpropagation neural network. Chawathe et al.11 used neural networks to predict gamma ray log from seismic attributes; amplitude, phase, frequency, reflection strength, and quadrature. However, they have used higher-resolution crosswell seismic data instead of surface seismic as a new approach. Soto and Holditch12 have used the same types of attributes from surface seismic to predict the gamma ray log with neural networks.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_13
blocks.text: Reeves et al.13 introduced a new methodology, which divides the whole seismic inversion problem into two parts. They have considered cross-well tomography as an intermediate step in their procedure, after finding a correlation between surface seismic and cross-well seismic. They have suggested producing virtual cross-well seismic data, before dealing with logs. Giving Chawathe et al.’s11 work as an example, they stated that well logs can easily be predicted from virtual cross-well seismic data. According to the authors, using crosswell seismic as an intermediate scale data can provide improved vertical resolution, increase constraints and reduce the uncertainty of reservoir description.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_14
blocks.text: In this study, a similar methodology is followed. Instead of cross-well seismic which is rather hard to obtain, vertical seismic profile (VSP) is incorporated into the study as the intermediate scale data. This is due to the fact that VSP is available more frequently, and is less expensive to obtain than cross-well tomography. It is a common type of data that can be found in many fields.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_15
blocks.text: Together with the integration of a third type of data, another unique feature of this study was developing and integrating a synthetic model to the research, before dealing with real data. Having a synthetic model that we had full control of gave us the opportunity to develop and test the proposed methodology better before applying it to real data. Our synthetic model represents the gas-producing Atoka and Morrow formations and the overlying Pennsylvanian sequence in the Buffalo Valley Field in New Mexico. Surface seismic and VSP responses of this model are computed. Artificial neural networks are used to develop two independent correlation models between; 1) Surface seismic and VSP, 2) VSP and well logs. Density log has been selected as the target log, and is predicted from the seismic line. In the second case, seismic field data have been used to predict gamma ray and neutron porosity distributions through a seismic section.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_16
blocks.text: In the following sections a theoretical background, which includes brief explanations of seismic surveys and artificial neural networks -under the light of the methodology of this studyare included. Then, the methodologies followed in the synthetic and the field cases are presented. After that, the results and their discussions are followed by conclusions.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_17
blocks.text: Theoretical Background

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_18
blocks.text: seismic Surveys. The seismic method is the most widely used tool in the exploration of hydrocarbon reservoirs. It is useful for obtaining a structural view of the subsurface geology. The basic theory of the seismic method is based on the movements of signals through the subsurface. Reflection method is the most widely used seismic method, which is useful in identifying formation tops. A seismic trace is the response of a single seismic detector to the seismic energy propagation through the earth. If these traces are displayed side-by-side, then it is called a seismic record. A processing stage comes after obtaining a seismic record, to enhance the signal, to minimize the noise and increase the resolution. These processed images are than compiled together to produce the final output of the seismic survey: a seismic section14.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_19
blocks.text: Vertical seismic profiling (VSP) differs from conventional seismic surveys in the location of signal receivers. In VSP surveys, the receivers are located in the borehole instead of at the earth’s surface. Because the earth acts as a low-pass filter, placing of the receivers at depth reduces the distance that the signal has to travel through the earth, thus yielding higher frequency (higher resolution) data. VSP surveys are very similar to velocity surveys in terms of where the sources and receivers are located. However, they differ from each other with two issues14:

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_20
blocks.text: The distance between geophone recording depths (smaller in VSP, every 15-40 meters)

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_21
blocks.text: Collection of information (Only first break times are collected in velocity surveys. In VSP, upgoing and downgoing events are also collected for several seconds.)

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_22
blocks.text: seismic attributes are all the information obtained from seismic data, either by direct measurements or by logical or experience-based reasoning15. The attributes used in this study can be briefly defined as;

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_23
blocks.text: Amplitude: Measure of the strength of the reflected signal. Indicates changes in physical properties of various lithological entities. It can sometimes be used to detect gas presence11.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_24
blocks.text: Hilbert Transform: This amounts to a 90-degree phase rotation. Amplitude and Hilbert transform are combined as Cartesian components of a trace signal16.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_25
blocks.text: Instantaneous Phase: Phase angles range from -180 degrees to +180 degrees. Envelope and phase are combined as polar components of a trace signal16.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_26
blocks.text: Average Energy: This attribute integrates the envelope between paraphase events. It highlights stratigraphic detail through energy fluctuations across traces. Values are in degrees16.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_27
blocks.text: Envelope: Represents the reflection strength. The envelope is independent of the phase and it relates directly to the acoustic impedance contrasts16.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_28
blocks.text: Frequency: This attribute describes how long it takes the phase to complete 360 degrees of rotation16.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_29
blocks.text: Paraphase: This attribute is the instantaneous phase with the predictable trend removed. As such, it assists visualizing the structural picture because phase tracks geologic boundaries16.

blocks.text: Figure 2 shows a typical neuron (processing element). Outputs (In) coming from another neuron are multiplied by their corresponding weights (Wn), and summed up. An activation function is then applied to the summation, and the output of that neuron is now calculated and ready to be transferred to another neuron18. There are many different types of neural network architectures and algorithms available. In this study, a generalized regression neural network (GRNN) is used. GRNN is a modification to probabilistic neural network that has been suggested by authors, who have studied seismic inversion8.9. GRNN has also been successfully used in geological pattern recognition applications such as synthetic log generation10 and total organic carbon content prediction from logs19. Besides, GRNN has been used in finding a correlation between cross-well seismic and surface seismic13.20. Huang et al.19 described GRNN as an easy-toimplement tool, which has efficient training capabilities, and the ability to handle incomplete patterns.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion

blocks.text: Generalized Regression Neural Network. Introduced by Specht21 in 1991, GRNN is a one-pass learning algorithm with a highly parallel structure. It is a memory-based network, which provides estimates of continuous variables, and converges to the underlying regression surface. This approach is freed from the necessity of assuming a specific functional form. Instead, the appropriate form is expressed as a probability density function (pdf), which can be determined from the observed data. General regression uses y (a scalar random variable), the X (a particular measured value of a vector random variable x), and the non-parametric estimator of the joint probability density function f(x, y). blocks.text: The estimate Y(X) is defined as a weighted average of the observed values, Yi, where each observed value is weighted exponentially according to its Euclidian or city block distance21. σ is the smoothing factor, and optimum smoothing factor is determined after several runs according to the meansquared error of the estimate, which must be kept at minimum. This process is referred to as the training of the network. If a number of iterations pass with no improvement in the meansquared error, that smoothing factor is determined as the optimum one for that data set. In the production phase, that smoothing factor is applied to data sets that the network has not seen before. While applying the network to a new set of data, increasing the smoothing factor would result in decreasing the range of output values.

It may have multidimensional input, and it will fit multidimensional surfaces through data22. It is a three-layer network. In the hidden layer, there must be one hidden neuron for each training pattern.

The positive amplitudes (blue in Figure 3) are produced at the top of the carbonates, reflecting the interface between an overlying weak acoustic impadance rock (shales, layers in white) and an underlying high acoustic impadance (carbonates). blocks.text: The data used is within the interval 0.8-1.124 seconds (6600-9000 ft.), as it represents a major exploration target in the area. Above this interval, there is seismic noise that was ignored as input data. In the following section, these two steps of correlation will be explained in details.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_95
blocks.text: Step 1: Correlation of Surface seismic with VSP: An effort was made to find a correlation between surface seismic attributes and VSP attributes. First, the model was visualized:

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_96
blocks.text: cross-sectional distributions of density, acoustic velocity and seismic attributes for both surface seismic and VSP were plotted.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_97
blocks.text: The main aim was to determine the most appropriate portion of the synthetic data set that should be used in training of the network. The success of a neural network model depends strongly on the way it is trained. Thus, the training data set must be representative of the geological complexity of the area being modeled. Only then, one can obtain successful results in the prediction phase. For this purpose, an effort was made to identify special geological features that can be useful in training the neural network. These include: edges of sand channels, extreme value points, and unique geological structures. In this particular case, those kinds of features could be found mostly in the central part of the synthetic seismic section. After several tests, we decided to use data of traces 32 and 57 (Figure 4). Because of the limitation in optimum number of data rows, only two traces were used for training.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_98
blocks.text: The network structure used in training is shown in Figure 5-a. As shown, data of traces 32 and 57 were used to predict a VSP attribute from time and seven available surface seismic attributes. At the end, seven separate prediction models have been developed for seven attributes. After having confidence of the prediction abilities of these models, they were applied to the whole seismic line to obtain network-predicted distributions of all the available seismic attributes. These attributes were then plotted in order to compare them with the actual ones.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_99
blocks.text: Step 2: Correlation of VSP with Well Logs: The second step of the correlation was deriving log properties from the neural network-derived VSP data. Since trace 50 is the trace which includes all of the data that we are dealing with (i.e. surface seismic, VSP and well logs), this trace was used to develop the model for this part of the correlation. The density log was selected as the target log.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_100
blocks.text: When one looks at the density log of trace 50, one can clearly see that there are a few different averaged values of density (Figure 6), which have been later defined as classes. Each of these classes actually represents a different type of rock layer defined in the model. Finally, instead of using actual values of density, it was decided to use these classes as the target values. By doing this, we have changed the nature of the neural modeling to one of classification. Classification networks are sometimes simpler than networks that are built to predict continuous values. In the initial trial; classes were defined as (Figure 6);

blocks.text: Case 2: Field Study (B. Valley Field, New Mexico) Available data. The following data were used in this study23:

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_104
blocks.text: A 3D seismic survey, loaned by WesternGeco for this study, covering an area of 24 mi2 with a vibroseis source,

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_105
blocks.text: sweep frequencies ranging from 8 to 98 Hz, and a sweep length of 17 seconds.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_106
blocks.text: A vertical seismic profile volume, with a two-LRS-315 vibrators source, covering an area of approximately 3.5 mi2 in the southeast corner of the area.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_107
blocks.text: Logs from around 40 wells were available as either paper or electronic copies. Available types of logs included gamma ray, neutron, density, sonic, spontaneous potential, and resistivity. Paper copies have been scanned, and then digitized together with other available electronic copies. Average total depth of those wells were ranging from 8000 to 9000 ft, intersecting the Atoka and Morrow formations.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_108
blocks.text: Unfortunately, not all of the available well logs were of high visual quality. That made them hard to accurately digitize. It is a proven fact that quality of the data has an important role in building reliable neural network models. Reasonable amount of noise in the data is acceptable, and even useful for a more realistic model. However, it is impossible to rely on a model, which has been built with unreliable data. Rolon’s study4 clearly states this fact, by comparing two similar studies with well log data having different levels of quality. Given these issues, the digitized log files were evaluated and selected for neural network design based on overall quality, to avoid building poor prediction models. Only good quality logs were used.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_109
blocks.text: Within the context of log quality and distribution, and the location of the VSP well, a seismic line (Figure 7) was extracted from the 3D survey area for use in the neural network design and evaluation. The line trends SE-NW through the survey area, and passes through five wells including the VSP well. The line included 173 seismic traces; the VSP well, well-1, located on trace 16 (Figure 7). Other wells are located on traces 55, 90, 123, and 153, respectively. The data shown in Figure 7 are seismic amplitudes.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_110
blocks.text: VSP data were available only for well-1. Surface seismic data used in the analysis extended from 0.92-1.1 seconds (twoway time). This interval includes reflection events associated with the Atoka-Morrow target interval A total of 27 seismic attributes were available. Eleven of these attributes were provided by the Kingdom Suite, and other 16 attributes were calculated using theoretical relationships. Additional attributes included a variety of derivatives, instantaneous energy, power and acceleration, quality factor, acoustic impedance inversions, and various residuals and smoothed outputs of other attributes.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_111
blocks.text: Methodology. The methodology as the one employed in the synthetic case study was followed in this case. Since there was only one available VSP survey (Well-1), the required correlation models for VSP prediction were restricted to data from that well. The seismic and attribute data were resampled to 0.0005 seconds (half-millisecond). Well log responses in depth were converted to time using modified well and surface seismic velocity functions. The log responses were also resampled to half-millisecond intervals.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_112
blocks.text: In the log prediction stage, the approach that has been carried out was to use all the available well data for training, and to apply the model to other parts of the seismic line to obtain the distributions. The main idea is to have a more

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_113
blocks.text: reliable training model by using all the available data. In this case, 90% of the total of 871 rows of data from five wells was used for training, while 10% was used for testing during training. Two types of logs: gamma ray and neutron porosity were selected as target logs. Because of the large number of available attributes a Key Performance Indicator (KPI) study was carried out, to determine the most influential attributes24. As a result of this study each attribute had a coefficient between 0 and 1, which basically shows the influence of that attribute on the selected output (i.e. logs). The attributes (including the time) were ranked based on their KPI coefficients and the ones having a coefficient larger than 0.5 were used as inputs. Those rankings for gamma ray and neutron porosity are shown in Table 3. The best thirteen attributes for the gamma ray, and the best eight attributes for the neutron porosity had coefficients higher than 0.5, and they were used as the input attributes. Training results were analyzed for each well separately, and upon applying those models to the other traces on the seismic line, distributions of gamma ray logs and neutron porosity logs were produced.

blocks.text: Results and Discussions

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_115
blocks.text: Case 1. Table 4 shows the correlation statistics of the training models developed for this step of the study. Correlation coefficient, r, and r-squared values are included as accuracy indicators of the match. Results for pattern (overall), training, calibration, and verification sets are included. Figure 8 shows the results of the training as actual vs. network-predicted plots for training, calibration, and verification sets of seven attributes. Each set of data is shown with a different symbol and color. Statistical and visual results indicate that reliable models have been developed. These models have been applied to the whole line (i.e. other traces of the synthetic model). The seismic attribute distributions have been re-produced. They have been re-plotted to be able to compare with the actual distributions. Figure 9-a shows the comparison plots for three attributes: amplitude, average energy, and envelope; and Figure 9-b shows the plots for three other attributes: frequency, Hilbert transform, and paraphase, which are obtained after applying the models for these attributes to the entire line. These plots also include the actual log lines of each attribute at traces 20, 35, 50, 65, and, 80, which makes it easier to assess the quality of the produced distributions.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_116
blocks.text: For the second step, where the density has been predicted; actual vs. network plot of the training model is shown in Figure 10-a. Although the network seemed to be successful in most parts, it has missed some points in the middle-valued region which was assumed to belong to Class 2: 2.3 g/cc. In order to overcome this problem, it has been decided to introduce another class to our model. Class 4 was assigned to density values around 2.09 g/cc (Figure 10-b). That has helped the network to be successful in that region (Figure 10-b), and this network model was chosen to be used in further studies. The correlation statistics of this model are shown in Table 5 together with the results for the velocity log. Actual VSP attributes were applied to this model, and density has been predicted along the seismic line with a correlation coefficient of 0.82. This has been repeated with the predicted VSP attributes coming from the first correlation step. The density has again been predicted through the seismic line with a

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_117
blocks.text: correlation coefficient value of 0.81. Figure 11 shows the final actual vs. network-predicted density distributions. It is seen that, the lithological units as well as the sand channels have been successfully predicted by the neural network. With this final result, the goal of predicting density log through the twostep intelligent seismic inversion methodology has been accomplished. The same procedure has also been applied to velocity and acoustic impedance.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_118
blocks.text: Case 2. As in the synthetic case, surface seismic – VSP correlation models have been developed, by using time and eleven surface seismic attributes to predict the single VSP attribute. The attributes used in this study were the ones which have been generated from the Kingdom Suite as the other attributes can be derived by using those ones. Table 6 shows the correlation statistics for these models for each attribute. Results for pattern, training, calibration, and verification sets are included. Verification results for phase, paraphase, frequency, and signed frequency seemed to be low. However, when plotted it seemed that they were not as bad as their correlation coefficients would suggest. Their actual vs. network graphs are shown in Figure 12. Actual vs. network plots for other attributes are shown in Figure 13. These models were then applied to other traces on the seismic line, with the available surface seismic data. VSP distributions were produced through the entire seismic line.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion

blocks.text: In the log prediction stage, gamma ray and neutron porosity were selected as the target logs. The results for these two types of logs are presented below separately.

blocks.text: Gamma Ray: Correlation statistics are shown in Table 7 for pattern, training, and testing sets, respectively. Results are showing both overall statistics, and separate well statistics. Graphs that show actual and network-predicted log lines are shown in Figure 14 for all wells. Figure 15 shows the predicted gamma ray distribution of the seismic line using these models. Actual log lines of five wells are also shown in the plot which may give a better perspective of comparisons.

blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_122
blocks.text: Conclusions

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_123
blocks.text: In this study, a novel approach to the seismic inversion problem is introduced. A two-scale-step, intelligent seismic inversion methodology is successfully implemented on a synthetic model, and real data of the Buffalo Valley Field, New Mexico. The main conclusions of this study can be summarized as follows:

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_124
blocks.text: Even being in a complex and non-linear manner, it was shown that a relationship does exist between various seismic attributes and reservoir properties. Such a relationship can be extracted by using artificial neural networks, one of the major soft computing tools. Generalized regression neural network (GRNN), which is a useful algorithm for approximating continuous functions, was applied successfully in this study.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_125
blocks.text: Benefits of using a synthetic seismic model were clearly seen in developing the appropriate methodology by identifying the most appropriate neural network algorithm and testing to use other tools. The synthetic model not only made it easy to be familiar with the type of data that is dealt with, but also provided the opportunity of comparing results for the whole seismic section. Although it was not applicable for the field study, the synthetic model was used for a classification (lithology identification) approach.

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_126
blocks.text: Although there are several examples of using artificial neural networks to correlate seismic attributes to reservoir properties, or well logs, this study is first of its kind simply because of integrating three types and scales of data (surface seismic, VSP, and well logs).

blocks.doc_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion
blocks.block_id: Reservoir Characterization Using Intelligent Seismic Inversion_127
blocks.text: To determine the data that should be used for training, model visualization can be helpful. It was seen in the first correlation step of the synthetic model study that; including diverse geological characteristics in the training set can increase the prediction abilities of the neural network models.
